# Deployment ledger  _(last tick 15:25 PT 2026-09-10 - HALT LIFTED: infra revision applied and independently re-verified (CT204 -> ptait07 keeping IP .162; billing CT100 -> CT120 on corsairai300 at .153); launcher restarted pid 60276 and immediately launched task 136 `4a3b0449` + BMAD 111 `cb75a2ba`, cap 2 full; capacity floor is PROVIDER exhaustion not infra - Synthetic 0 tokens for the week, 7/7 Ollama Cloud keys LIMIT, local ornith healthy at 0.5s (was 72s before the rebuild))_ the /goal is not met until every row reads VERIFIED.

A task is **not done** when its harness run finishes. It is done when the change is
**live in the environment it targets and that has been confirmed by reading the live system.**

States, in order. A row only advances on evidence, never on assumption:

| State | What it means | Evidence required to claim it |
|---|---|---|
| QUEUED | entry exists in C:/tmp/queue | the file |
| RUNNING | a harness run is executing it | run id, status running |
| GATED | run is at an approval gate | approval id + the completion report |
| BRANCHED | **committed locally and nothing more** | `git log origin/<base>..HEAD` |
| PUSHED | the branch is **on the remote** | `git ls-remote origin <branch>` / the remote sha |
| PR | pull request open | PR number + `diff --stat` |
| REVIEWED | a review was posted AND acted on | the review text, and what changed because of it |
| MERGED | merged to the target branch | merge commit sha |
| LANE | its deploy lane ran | lane run id + per-job conclusions |
| LIVE | the change is in the target environment | a probe of the LIVE system showing the new behaviour |
| VERIFIED | proven, not assumed | the specific command/response that proves it |

Four OFF-PATH states are legal. Use them rather than improvising a word:

| State | What it means | Must record |
|---|---|---|
| HELD | deliberately not advancing (capacity, quiet window, owner gate) | WHY |
| BLOCKED | cannot advance until something else lands | WHAT, by name |
| FAILED | the attempt ran and did not succeed | the CAUSE, not the symptom |
| SUPERSEDED | another task owns this work now | WHICH task |

**Do not invent a state.** COMMITTED is not one - that is BRANCHED. DONE is not one either - say
MERGED, LANE, LIVE or VERIFIED, whichever the evidence actually supports.
**BRANCHED vs PUSHED is a real distinction**: a run that commits and stops is BRANCHED, and
finishing it is the overseer job; a branch held back by a deliberate override is a different
situation and must not be "finished" by accident. The state says which.

Rows here are updated every tick. If a row cannot advance, record WHY in Blocker.

Full suite reads `9 failed | 47 passed` - but the next line is `225 passed (225)`. **Zero tests

## TICK 16:30 PT 2026-09-09 - TASKS 79 + OUTAGE LOG MERGED; A RED E2E TEST FOUND HIDING INSIDE A GREEN GATE

### Both PRs merged and read back on main

    PR #128  task 79, Pi-hole allowlist      infrastructure/pihole/apply-allowlist.sh   16,643 bytes on main
    PR #127  provider outage log             .../Services/OutageLogService.cs            4,671 bytes on main

Checked BEFORE merging that neither touches `infrastructure/litellm-config.yaml`, so no prod-router
force-recreate and the four live runs were never at risk. Lane `34415612962` (#128) came back
**all six jobs green**, including Deploy to CT202 and QA Verify (prod). #127's lane still running.

### THE FINDING: the E2E Gate reports SUCCESS while a test inside it FAILS

    ✗ [26-fleet-dns-tls.test.js] 26B - Caddy *.lan wildcard TLS  route pihole/ is served
      pihole.lan.easybutt0n.ai/: network error: fetch failed - hard failure under RUN_LIVE_REGRESSION

A test explicitly labelled **"hard failure"** sitting inside a job whose conclusion is **success**.
That is the read-a-rollup-as-health trap, and it is worth fixing on its own: a gate that reports
green while carrying a hard failure cannot be trusted as a gate.

**NOT caused by the merge** - enumerated rather than assumed. The same test fails in the two prior
lanes, `34404894107` (21:09) and `34389898842` (18:39), both of which were green overall. It is
pre-existing and has been passing through unnoticed.

### Root cause - fully diagnosed, and the TEST IS RIGHT

First probe was from the wrong vantage: corsairai300 has **no A record at all** for the host, so
everything returned 000 there. That is the "tested a different path than the one failing" trap.
Re-probed from **CT210, the runner that actually executes the suite**:

    pihole.lan.easybutt0n.ai   -> 192.168.21.3    (the Pi-hole itself)
    pi-hole.lan.easybutt0n.ai  -> 192.168.21.161  (Caddy)  -> 404, which the test EXPECTS and passes
    ops.lan.easybutt0n.ai      -> 192.168.21.161  (Caddy)

    192.168.21.3:443 is OPEN and presents:
        subject = CN = pi.hole
        issuer  = CN = pi.hole, O = Pi-hole, C = DE      <- self-signed
    curl from CT210: http=000, ssl_verify=19 (unable to get issuer cert locally)

**A specific DNS A record for `pihole` shadows the `*.lan.easybutt0n.ai` wildcard.** The wildcard
points at Caddy on .161; the specific record sends `pihole` straight to the Pi-hole on .3, which
answers 443 with its own self-signed certificate. So the Caddy route the test asserts can never be
served, and the failure is honest.

### Two options, and this is PAXTON'S CALL - I have not touched DNS

  (a) **Remove the specific `pihole` A record** so the wildcard applies and Caddy serves it, which
      is what the test asserts and what every other `*.lan` host does.
  (b) **The test's expectation is wrong** - if `pihole.lan` is deliberately a direct-to-admin
      shortcut, the assertion should be that it serves the Pi-hole, not that Caddy routes it.

I did not change anything because this is LAN DNS on the PRIMARY Pi-hole, and the recorded hazard
is that **the `dns.hosts` setter REPLACES the whole list** rather than appending - so a careless
write there takes out every other LAN name. See memory `lan-dns-two-piholes`.

**Separately worth fixing regardless of which option wins:** the E2E Gate job must not conclude
`success` while a test it ran is a hard failure. That is the more dangerous half of this finding.

## TICK 14:52 PT 2026-09-09 - IT WAS MY MERGE. FOUND, FIXED, PROVEN AGAINST THE LIVE ROUTER. PR #28.

**I was wrong at 14:16 and the entry below it is retracted.** #27 did not only touch error
classification - it also rewrote `litellm-acceptance/test-litellm-router.test.js`, and that
rewrite is what took the mcp-tools QA gate down. `infra=0` correctly ruled out a
*classification* bug; extending that to "not my merge" was the error.

### The tell I nearly walked past

    not ok 1 - POST /v1/chat/completions returns content for qwen3.5:27b
      duration_ms: 13.420857
      error: "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'get')"

**13 milliseconds and a JavaScript TypeError.** No network call takes 13 ms. Once I read the
duration instead of the message, the provider theory was dead.

### Two defects, not one

`request()` (test-litellm-router.test.js:62) returns a **plain object** - there is no
`.headers` on it; the `x-litellm-*` headers are pre-extracted into `res.litellmHeaders`:

    return { status, elapsed, bodyText, json, parseError, contentType, deploymentHint, litellmHeaders };

`validateServedModel()`, new in #27, called `res.headers.get('x-litellm-model-id')`. That
threw on every response, at both call sites (chat completions and messages).

**Behind it sat a second defect that would have survived the first fix.** The check asserted
`x-litellm-model-id === requestedModel`. Probed against the UAT router (CT204, LiteLLM
1.100.0), on **both** routes:

    body.model              qwen3.5:27b
    x-litellm-model-group   qwen3.5:27b     <- the header that carries the model NAME
    x-litellm-model-id      38fa92ff...112e <- a 64-hex DEPLOYMENT hash, never a model name

So `model-id` never equals a model name, and the assertion would have failed **every request**
even with the shape corrected. The fix reads `x-litellm-model-group` out of `litellmHeaders`.

### Why CI could not have caught it - the part worth keeping

#27 also shipped `test-served-model-readback.test.js`: 6 unit tests, all green in the same
failing run. They were green because the file **copy-pasted the implementation** and mocked
`res.headers.get(...)` - a shape `request()` never returns. **A test that validated a
duplicate of the code against a fabricated input, and could not fail.**

The implementation now lives **once**, in `packages/runner/src/litellm-matrix.mjs` beside
`litellmHeaderNames`; the acceptance test and the unit test both import it. The duplicate
cannot drift again. Added a regression guard that a fetch-Response-shaped object is rejected
by the body check rather than throwing a TypeError.

### Proof - RULE 1, tested the fix rather than re-reading the diff

Ran the real patched test file against the **live UAT router**, not a mock:

**The control is what makes this trustworthy**: a string known to be on the page returns 4, so the
method finds what is there. All five new strings are present in
`/app/OpsControlCenter.dll` inside the RUNNING container.

**So #123's code is VERIFIED in the deployed artifact** - read out of the binary, not inferred from a

success, deploy failure, 90-minute timeout, or an unhandled exception. The old script did not guarantee
that. There is also a hard **90-minute cap** - if the runs have not finished by then it resumes the
launcher and does NOT deploy.

### THE DIFF SCARE - and why "check diff --stat before every PR" earns its place

Before opening the PR I ran the standing check and got:

    417 files changed, 22614 insertions(+), 1093197 deletions(-)

**Over a million deleted lines**, including `tests/`, `skills/`, `scripts/` - for what was supposed to
be a single plan document. I stopped rather than opening it.

It was a **diverged-base artifact**, not a deletion:

    main ahead by: 218    branch ahead by: 1
    merge-base: 5b908a5
    diff vs merge-base: docs/runbooks/ptait07-root-capacity-plan.md | 230 ++++++  (1 file, +230)

The branch's base is **218 commits behind main**, so a tip-to-tip diff reports main's own additions as
the branch's deletions. GitHub renders the **merge-base** diff, so the PR itself is correct - one file.

**Both halves of this matter.** The check caught something that looked catastrophic, and then the
follow-up stopped me reporting a false alarm. `git diff A B` against a stale branch is not the branch's
change; `git diff $(git merge-base A B) B` is. Recorded in the PR body so nobody re-runs the same scare.

Secret scan on the added lines: clean, env NAMES only (`LAN_DEPLOY_SSH_KEY` referenced by name).

then re-run.** A retry is only safe when the failure was transient; this one had left the host in a
state the pipeline could not reason about. Queued as **task 85** so the pipeline catches a name
collision *before* it half-applies a production deploy.

### THE MERGE WINDOW RULE, SETTLED FROM THE WORKFLOW SOURCE

I have argued both sides of this today. It is now read from `.github/workflows/deploy-mcp-tools.yml`
rather than inferred from behaviour, and **both halves are true at once**:

    deploy:
      name: Deploy to CT202
      needs: [e2e-tests, qa-gate-uat]        # <- NO `environment:` key

    - name: Recreate litellm-router if config changed
      if: steps.sync_infra_files.outputs.LITELLM_CONFIG_CHANGED == '1'

and `LITELLM_CONFIG_CHANGED` is set by comparing **sha256 of the deployed `litellm-config.yaml`
before and after the sync**. So:

1. The prod deploy job runs on **every** merge to main. (My correction was right.)
2. The router recreate is gated on the config file's **content hash**. (My original rule was right.)
3. It is a content hash, not a git diff - so a comment-only edit still recreates, which matches the

## TICK 10:28 PT 2026-09-09 - THE PROD ROUTER "CRASH" IS A SPEND-LOGGING BUG, NOT A REQUEST-PATH FAULT

I chased `CT202 liveliness=000` to the end rather than leaving it at "healthy now". The conclusion

### What the 495 errors actually are

The traceback head - which my earlier grep failed to capture - is:

    File ".../litellm/llms/openai/openai.py", line 1067, in async_streaming
    -> spend_log_error_logger.py:81 - Error creating spendlogs object - maximum recursion depth exceeded
    -> File "/usr/lib/python3.13/copy.py", line 222, in _deepcopy_dict
    -> TypeError: cannot pickle '_thread.RLock' object

The spend logger deep-copies the request object to build a SpendLogs row. For **streaming** requests
that object holds a live client handle containing an `RLock`, which `deepcopy` cannot pickle. The
request itself is already served by then. Counts over the same 2h window:

| signature | count |
|---|---|
| `HTTPException in MCP tool call: 403 User not allowed to call this tool` | 6529 |
| `router async_function_with_fallbacks` error | 845 |
| `Spend tracking - update_database failed` | 533 |
| `Error creating spendlogs object - maximum recursion depth exceeded` | 533 |
| `cannot pickle '_thread.RLock'` | 495 |
| **HTTP 500/502/503 responses** | **2** |
| **HTTP 200 responses** | **8422** |

8422 successes against 2 failures. The router is not dropping traffic. **NOT AN INCIDENT.**

### But it does invalidate a number I published today

I ranked model usage from `LiteLLM_SpendLogs` earlier today, after correctly rejecting `/spend/logs`
as a proxy. If streaming spend rows fail to insert, that table is **systematically missing streaming
traffic** - which is most harness traffic. The ranking is not trustworthy and I am withdrawing it
rather than leaving it standing. Queued as task 82.

## TICK 07:22 PT - THE THIRD PIPELINE FAULT FIXED: uat NEVER DEPLOYED. PR #98

No launch capacity this tick - Synthetic 429 on 3 of 3 sampled models, and the local span is held by
822dee5d (round 4/14, executor active). 13 tasks queued and unable to start. So rather than idle, I fixed
the fault I had already diagnosed and which needs no harness capacity.

**The fault.** `release-ff` pushes `release`, and ci.yml deploys on push to `[main, develop, release]`, so
the uat lane was expected to roll itself. It never fired: **GitHub does not trigger workflows from pushes
made with the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN`** - its recursion guard - and release-ff pushes with exactly that.
Branch moves, no lane runs, uat keeps serving an older build, and `wait-uat` goes green anyway. A false
green sitting directly in front of production.

**Ruled out the obvious alternative rather than assuming.** `LAN_DEPLOY_ENABLED` is `1` - read from the
repo variables this tick, so that is NOT the cause. The dev lane deploys correctly because merges to
`develop` are pushed with a real user credential; the suppression is specific to the branches the
promotion pushes itself (`release`, `prod`).

**Fix: PR #98.** A `uat-deploy` job between `release-ff` and `wait-uat`, on the same
`[self-hosted, lan-deploy]` runner, calling the same `scripts/deploy/rollout.sh` with lane `uat` - exactly
what the `production` job already did. `wait-uat` now `needs: uat-deploy`, so the gate cannot be polled
before the build it judges is deployed. No duplicated deploy logic: both jobs call the one script. YAML
parses; job graph `dev-check -> release-ff -> uat-deploy -> wait-uat -> production`.

**This is the THIRD fault in this one pipeline with the same shape** - #96 (deploy applied, verification
timed out, reported failure), #97 (deploy succeeded, gate polled an empty sha and crashed), #98 (branch
moved, nothing deployed, gate reported success). Every one of them made the recorded outcome disagree with
what was actually running. That is the pattern worth stamping out: a pipeline that reports an outcome it did
not achieve teaches everyone to ignore it.

**Task 66 NARROWED, not cancelled.** It is broader than #98 - its heart is a post-deploy version assertion
at EVERY stage plus CI-guard tests, which #98 does not add. Appended a delta to
`billing-promotion-uat-never-deploys-task.txt`: what #98 already lands (do not redo, do not open a competing
PR), the fact that `rollout.sh` already asserts version==tag so uat gains that assertion for the first time,
the two facts measured today (`LAN_DEPLOY_ENABLED=1`; dev works because of the credential), and what remains
- the promotion-level assertion covering skipped stages, the dev stage, task 65's health-`status` half, and
the tests. Narrowing, not a new slice.

**Watchdog fix holding.** Two cycles logged this tick against 822dee5d on the single-slot span: "Reporting
only", no abort. That is the correct behaviour and the run is still alive at round 4.

requeued as `710-68-ct110-capacity.json` after two failed probes of `kimi-k3:synthetic-anthropic`.

That was wrong. Synthetic was 429 on **7 of 7 models fleet-wide** at that moment; the run itself was healthy,
four rounds in, carrying the host measurements I had gathered by hand and injected minutes earlier.

**The flaw, exactly.** The watchdog has a provider-outage guard meant to prevent this:
`if suspects and len(suspects) > max(1, len(live) // 2)`. With **one** live run that is `1 > 1` - **always
false**. So a single run on an exhausted provider was ALWAYS aborted; the guard could never fire at n=1.

The deeper error is one I keep writing rules about and then committing: **inferring provider health from how
many of our runs happen to be affected is a sample of one dressed up as a population.** The number of affected
runs is a proxy, and this is the third time a proxy in this watchdog has cost real work (`ever_worked` was the
first two).

**Fix: measure the provider, do not count the victims.** When a probe fails on a `:synthetic` model, probe a
DIFFERENT model on the same provider as a control. If the control also fails, the provider is down and this run
is a bystander - report, do not abort - whatever the live-run count. Patched `spin_watchdog.py`, `ast.parse`
clean, backup kept at `spin_watchdog.py.bak-*`. **Restarted the watchdog** so the fix is actually live rather
than sitting in a file (the running process held the old code); confirmed exactly one watchdog process and its
first cycle logged correctly, single-slot rule reporting-only on 822dee5d.

`ct110-capacity-task.txt` so the relaunch does not stop to ask the same four questions again - that narrows the
task, it does not add a slice.

## TWO PIPELINE DEFECTS FOUND BY WATCHING THE PROMOTION, BOTH REAL

**1. uat never deploys - task 66's ROOT CAUSE, now proven.** `release` IS at `702cc2f`, but the newest CI run
on release is `b9b06b7` from 23:54. No workflow fired for the fast-forward. Cause: the push is made with
`GITHUB_TOKEN`, and **GitHub does not trigger workflows from pushes made with that token** (recursion
guard). So the uat lane never deploys the build, and the `billing-uat` gate goes green anyway - a **false
green**. uat is still on `sha-b9b06b7` and still returns 500 to an unsigned POST, while dev and prod are on
702cc2f and return 400. I approved prod anyway and said so in the approval comment, because the change was
verified by BEHAVIOUR on dev (400 vs 500), not because I trusted the uat gate. Task 66 now has its cause;
the fix is a PAT or a deploy key for that push, or dispatching the uat deploy explicitly.

**2. The prod QA gate polled an EMPTY sha and crashed - PR #97.** The production job reads
`steps.ff.outputs.sha` twice, but the step with `id: ff` emits no such output; the `echo "sha=..."` line lives
in the `deploy` step. Log: `sha=""`, then
`jq: error (at <stdin>:5): Cannot index string with string "context"`, exit 5. So (a) the gate was dispatched
with an empty `caller_sha` and had no commit to report against, and (b) the poll built `/commits//statuses`,
GitHub returned an error OBJECT, and `.[]` iterated its string values. **A production deploy that had already
succeeded was recorded as a failed promotion.** Same class as #96: the pipeline disagreeing with what is
actually running. Fixed to use `inputs.ref` (required, and prod is fast-forwarded to exactly it), plus an
`if type == "array"` guard on all three polls so a transient API error retries instead of killing the job.

**Open PRs on mcp-cognizioware: #97** (this). Merged this tick: #95, #96.

## PAXTON WAS RIGHT: I WAS VERIFYING THE WRONG PIPELINE (06:50 PT 2026-09-10)

I merged the Stripe fix to `develop` and treated that as progress toward VERIFIED. Paxton asked "arent you
verifying the right pipelines?" **He was right and I was wrong.** `develop` feeds the **dev** lane only. The
endpoint Stripe actually calls is PROD - CT100 = 192.168.21.153 on ptait01. Merging to develop does not put
one byte of the fix on it.

**The real path, read from `.github/workflows/promote-billing.yml`:**
push develop -> dev lane + `cognizioware-qa/billing-dev` gate -> **dispatch `promote-billing` with the SHA**
-> fast-forward `release` -> uat + `billing-uat` gate -> `production` environment job -> fast-forward `prod`
-> `rollout.sh` -> `billing-prod` gate. The dispatch is a separate manual step I had not touched.

**And that pipeline is BROKEN - which is why prod is pinned to an older build than dev or uat.** Every recent
`promote-billing` run failed: five on 09-08, one cancelled 09-09. Cause, read from run 34248493870:

```
Container mcp-billing-service Recreated      16:04:36
!!! [prod] FAILED - health reports '', expected 'sha-9d0a6ca'   16:06:20
```

`scripts/deploy/rollout.sh` step 5 allows `20 x 5s = 100s` for the container to report its version. The
billing service's cold start is longer - it burns up to 30s on the secondary-DB connection timeout before
falling back to primary-only and serving. **The deploy applied correctly and then failed verification anyway.**
Worse than a red lane: the rollout APPLIES the change and then reports failure, so the recorded outcome
disagrees with what is actually running. Proven healthy today: `/api/health` on 192.168.21.153:20251 returns
`{"version":"sha-9d0a6ca"}`, 200.

**Fix: PR #96** -> develop. `seq 1 20` -> `seq 1 60` (100s -> 300s), plus a comment recording why the window
exists. It only ever waits longer before declaring failure; the exit condition is still an exact version match,
so it cannot turn a real failure into a pass. `bash -n` passes.

**ORDERING THAT MATTERS - do not get this wrong next tick.** The production job does `actions/checkout` with
`ref: prod` and runs `scripts/deploy/rollout.sh` **from the promoted SHA**. So promoting the Stripe fix
(`ee321ad`) on its own would run the OLD 100s rollout and fail again. #96 must merge FIRST; then promote the
develop HEAD that contains both. Sequence: merge #96 -> wait `billing-dev` green on the new HEAD ->
`promote-billing` with `is_production=true` -> approve the `production` environment -> read
`/api/health` version back AND re-probe the webhook (unsigned POST must return 400, not 500).

**Status of the Stripe work after this tick:** PR #95 MERGED to develop (`ee321ad`), CI in progress. It is
**LANE at best, NOT LIVE and NOT VERIFIED.** The live endpoint still runs sha-9d0a6ca without the fix. The
reconciliation of the 6 lost events IS live and verified - that was done directly against prod, not through
a lane.

## STRIPE WEBHOOK 500s - Paxton's forwarded email. DIAGNOSED, RECONCILED, FIXED (06:40 PT 2026-09-10)

Stripe warned that `https://mcp-cognizioware.easybutt0n.ai/api/v1/stripe/webhook` returned **HTTP 500 fourteen
times** since 2026-09-06 11:12:37 UTC and would stop delivering by 2026-09-15. Paxton asked whether our work
caused it. **It did not** - and the honest answer needed the live system, not the code.

**What actually happened: a 57-hour outage, not a webhook fault.** `http_request_response_logs` on CT100 has a
hard gap - zero requests of any kind from 2026-09-06 02:xx to 2026-09-08 11:00, spanning the CT100 reboot at
09-07 18:16. Stripe's first failure sits inside it. The service was simply not there.

**What was NOT wrong**, each read from the live system rather than assumed:
- The signing secret is correct. Enabled endpoint `we_1Tzb8d` (created 2026-08-01) matches the configured
  `Stripe__WebhookSecret`; it delivered 78 x 200 through 08-18. (A second endpoint on the same URL,
  `we_1TsXvM`, is **disabled** - harmless, but worth knowing it exists.)
- The endpoint is healthy NOW: a correctly signed event through the **public** URL returns
  `200 {"received":true,"duplicate":true}` - full Cloudflare -> origin -> DB path, the exact path Stripe uses.
  So the 09-15 disable threat is already resolved; new deliveries succeed.
- `stripe_webhook_events` has **zero** rows with Status='failed', in its entire history.

**Two measurement traps I walked into and got out of:**
1. I first "reproduced" the 500 with an unsigned POST and nearly reported that as the cause. It is a real bug
   (below) but it is NOT what Stripe hit - Stripe always sends the header.
2. I looked for the 500s in `http_request_response_logs` and found none, and briefly read that as "the requests
   never arrived". Wrong: **unhandled** exceptions bypass the logging middleware entirely. Proven by my own
   probe - the 405 and 400 from the same second were logged, the 500 was not. Absence there is not absence.

**The real bug this turned up (separate from the outage).** Both `StripeWebhookController` and
`GuestWebhookController` passed `Request.Headers["Stripe-Signature"]` straight to Stripe.net. Absent header ->
null -> `ParseStripeSignature` throws `NullReferenceException`, which is **not** a `StripeException`, so it
escaped the only catch and surfaced as an unhandled **500**. That matters because Stripe counts 5xx toward
disabling an endpoint: any unsigned scanner hitting this public URL inflates the failure count against a
healthy service. Fixed to return 400, plus a regression test. **PR #95** -> develop. Build clean, 6/6 tests pass.

**Reconciliation done.** Six events were lost in the outage window and Stripe had exhausted its retries (still
`pending_webhooks=1` after 26h of healthy service - it was never going to redeliver them). All six are
**test-mode** (`livemode: false`): three test customers, each a `customer.subscription.updated` plus a $39.00
`invoice.paid` - the **month-2 renewal** cycle, one month on from the August trial conversion. The three
subscriptions already existed as `active`, so no provisioning re-triggered; the gap was renewal accounting.
Replayed all six against the origin with valid signatures: **6 x 200**, all now `processed` with no Error, and
`LastStripeEventAtUtc` advanced from 2026-08-06 to 2026-09-06. Verified by reading the table back.

**NEW FINDING -> task 74 (appended at the END; the order is Paxton's).** `CurrentPeriodEndUtc` is still null on
all three subscriptions after processing. Cause read from the live payload: on api_version
`2025-09-30.clover` Stripe no longer sends `current_period_end` at subscription level - it is on
`items.data[].current_period_end` (confirmed present: 2026-10-06). So `UpsertSubscription` reads null and
renewal/expiry tracking never populates. This did NOT cause the email, so I did not fold it into PR #95.

## PROD ROUTER: A 502 TRACED TO A REAL, MEASURED FAULT (22:40 PT)

A routine liveliness probe returned **502**. It was not the deploy - that had only reached "Apply LiteLLM config to
**UAT CT204**" and never touched CT202. What actually happened:
 - The prod router container had **restarted** (`RestartCount=1`, `exit=0`) and was `health: starting`. Its own log
   showed `/health/liveliness 200 OK` internally, so the 502 was the edge during ~30-60s of restart. It is
   **healthy and serving 200 again**, confirmed twice.
 - The cause is not a one-off: `TypeError: cannot pickle '_thread.RLock' object` appears **4877 times in 6 hours**
   (~13/min).
 - Chain of causation, read off the logs: Ollama Cloud weekly limit -> every `:cloud` request raises RateLimitError
   -> `router.py:7024 async_function_with_fallbacks()` tries the chain -> **`glm-5.3-flash:cloud` is the FIRST rung
   in essentially every cloud chain** (the cheapest-first design at config line 260) and is itself exhausted -> the
   fallback lands on another 429 -> a deepcopy in that path hits an un-picklable RLock and throws.
 - **TWO Ollama accounts are exhausted, not one**: the errors name `prax211` AND `ai-dev02`.
**Deliberately NOT rewriting production fallback chains at this hour** with six runs live and two deploys mid-flight.
It is noisy rather than breaking - the router serves, the harness no longer uses those models, and the root trigger is
a spend decision already with Paxton. Folded the fix into task **64** (which already owns repointing) rather than
opening yet another task, with the caveat stated in the brief: repointing stops us TRIGGERING the bug; the deepcopy
fault itself is very likely a LiteLLM defect in the pinned version.
**Not zero-impact though:** a restart drops in-flight requests, so this cost some run traffic tonight.

**A HABIT OF MINE TO STOP: I keep eyeballing elapsed time and getting it wrong.** Three times this session -
twice on tick labels that drifted ~16 minutes ahead of the clock, and once just now, when I called the E2E gate
"45+ minutes and possibly stuck". It had started `05:16:54Z` against a clock of `05:33:43Z`: **17 minutes**. And the
workflow already bounds it - job timeout 45m, step timeout 35m for the advisory suite, warning at 25m - so it was
never able to hang, and the step is advisory anyway; the gate that decides, "local models MUST serve inference",
had already passed. Nothing was wrong except my arithmetic. **Rule for the rest of this session: never state an
elapsed time without subtracting two real timestamps.** A false "it's been 45 minutes" is how a healthy job gets
killed - the same error class as killing a slow-but-working run, which the watchdog was built to prevent.
**Watchdog decaying exactly as designed:** 60s -> 96s -> 153s across three clean passes.

**THE PROBE IS NOW ADAPTIVE (Paxton: "emits in the beginning and then slowly dies off until more abnormal or errors
happen").** My fixed 5-minute poll was wrong in BOTH directions at once: while the fleet is healthy it spends real
requests to learn nothing - and each probe is a request against a pack capped at 2500 per 5 hours, so the watchdog
can quietly eat the budget it exists to protect - while in the minutes that actually matter, just after a launch or
just after a break, five minutes is far too slow.
**Cadence now:** floor 60s, x1.6 per clean pass, ceiling 1200s - reaching the ceiling about 43 minutes into a quiet
stretch (60s, 96s, 153s, 244s, 390s, 624s, 998s, 1200s).
**Snaps straight back to 60s on any of:** a failed probe, a **SLOW** probe (>1.8s while still under the 3.0s budget),
a newly failed run, or a newly launched run. Slowness counting as abnormal is deliberate - a backend drifting from
1s to 2.5s is the early warning that precedes a timeout, and waiting for outright failure throws that warning away.
A newly launched run pulling the cadence to the floor is the "emits in the beginning" half: a bad binding shows
itself in the first minutes.
**Live:** `22:30:37 adaptive watchdog up ... 22:30:40 clean (6 live) -> backing off 60s to 96s`.

## THE EMIT PROBE NOW RUNS MID-ROUND, NOT JUST AT LAUNCH (Paxton's call, 22:45 PT)

> "cant we detect this with our emit probe? if the local model is just spinning then switch to the flash provider."

**The gap he spotted is real.** The probe ran exactly ONCE, at launch. It proved a backend answered before a round was
committed and then never looked again - so a round that starts healthy and spins for the full 1800s was invisible
until half an hour was gone. Task 63 showed both shapes tonight on the SAME pools: r0 executor timed out at
1800045 ms, r1 completed normally at 1151587 ms. At minute ten those are indistinguishable from outside.
**`C:/tmp/spin_watchdog.py` closes it.** Every 5 minutes, for any run whose current round has been going past a 900s
grace, it re-probes THAT RUN'S BOUND EXECUTOR:
  - long round + backend cannot emit  -> STARVED -> abort and requeue, so the launcher's rotation hands it a
    different trio with a flash executor. (Role bindings cannot be changed on a live run, which is why "switch to
    the flash provider" is implemented as requeue-onto-a-different-trio rather than a live swap.)
  - long round + backend answers in ~1s -> WORKING -> left completely alone.
**The probe, not the clock, makes the decision** - the clock only decides when to ask. A model thinking hard must
never be killed for being slow.
Safety built in: TWO consecutive failed probes before acting; never touches a gated run; and it **refuses to act at
all if more than half the live runs look starved**, because that pattern is a provider outage and mass-aborting would
turn an outage into lost work. Runs launched before this change have no recorded bindings and are skipped entirely,
so nothing already in flight can be wrongly killed.
Supporting change: the launcher now records `roles_bound` per run at launch - without it a watchdog would have to
GUESS which backend a long round is using, and guessing is how a working run gets killed.
**Live and verified:** dry-run first (round elapsed computed at 198-667s across 6 runs, all under grace, none
touched), then started - first pass reports `no starved executors (6 live)`.

**Paxton also asked for the emit readings in the web UX.** Folded into task **70** rather than made a new surface:
the outage log answers *what broke and when*, the emit readings answer *is it healthy right now*, and splitting them
across two pages is the exact failure that page exists to fix. The added brief specifies showing the alias AND the
model actually served (they differ - `kimi-k3:cloud` is served by `glm-5.3-flash:cloud`), time-to-first-token with
the budget shown, which role each model serves, unhealthy first, and staleness stated rather than hidden. It also
carries the three calibration traps that cost real time tonight, and forbids the page probing on render - that would
bill a request per model per page load against a 2500-per-5-hours pack.

**MODEL DOCTRINE SET BY PAXTON, 21:35-21:45 PT - and the economics behind it change the design.**
> "Synthetic doesn't differentiate which model uses the request... why would you be using the cheaper models?

Synthetic bills a REQUEST, not a model: 2500 per 5 hours is consumed identically by a flagship or a mid-tier
model. So spending a Synthetic request on a cheap model is waste - the slot must carry the strongest model
available, and cheap work belongs on the free local GPUs. The previous pools had glm-5.2, nemotron-3-super and
syn:large:vision in them, each burning a full-price request. All removed.
NEW TRIOS: manager = FLASH (glm-5.3-flash), executor = LOCAL qwen3.8-nothink first and FLASH cloud when local
cannot answer, auditor = FRONTIER (kimi-k3 / syn:large:text). CAP=6, no trio collapses, every backend inside
its limit: glm-5.3-flash:syn-a 5/5, glm-5.3-flash:cloud 5, kimi-k3 3/5, syn:large:text 3/5, qwen3.8-nothink 2/2.

**A SECOND SYNTHETIC PACK WOULD ROUGHLY DOUBLE THE MODEL CEILING - but CT110 becomes the next constraint.**
Model side: 6 backends x ~2 concurrent per model per pack = 12 role-slots / 3 roles = 4 runs (CAP=4 is exactly that);
a second pack gives 24 slots = 8 runs, and doubles the 1000-requests-per-5-hours budget, which matters across a
19-task queue. Harness side: no independent concurrency cap on CT110 (systemd unit and config both clean; the
`maxConcurrentRuns: 5` is Hydra's scheduling hint and Hydra is not launching these). Machine side: CT110 is
**4 vCPU / 6 GB**; at 4 runs it carries 10 claude processes at load ~1.4 (35%) and 1 GB used, so 8 runs means ~20
processes at load ~2.8 and 2-3 GB. **Realistic gain: 4 -> 6-7 runs, not a clean 8.** Conditions: it must be a separate
PACK, not another token on the same account, and each model needs a duplicate deployment carrying the second key so
LiteLLM load-balances across both.

## Tick 06:14 - the watchdog fix proved itself, and my "reliable" progress measure turned out not to be
Synthetic **429** on the 10th consecutive probe. Task 63 still the only run, r1.
**The watchdog's 04:50 rule fired for the first time and did the right thing:**
```
822dee5d probe failed on qwen3.8-nothink - SINGLE-SLOT backend, so the probe queues behind the
executor it is testing and cannot tell busy from starved. Reporting only; the 1800s episode budget
is the real guard here.
```
Reported, did not abort. Under the pre-04:50 code this run would have been killed - the third healthy casualty.
**Then a measure I documented an hour ago failed under me.** I had written "judge progress by the agent's elapsed
time". Reading it this tick: `ps` reported **4123168608 seconds - about 130 years - for EVERY process**, including
the `ps` and `bash` of my own command. Not a stalled agent; a broken counter.
**Diagnosed rather than worked around:** wall clocks are FINE and agree to one second across container, host and
this PC (13:14:46Z / 13:14:47Z / 13:14:47Z). But `/proc/stat`'s **`btime` disagrees with `/proc/uptime`** on
CT110, and `ps etimes` is derived from `btime`. So elapsed-time accounting is broken on that box while
wall-clock time is correct - a distinction that matters, because the harness's own budgets are wall-clock.

## Tick 05:00 - PR #101 was DIRTY on arrival; I resolved the conflict myself and it is MERGED
Opening #101 was premature: it came up **DIRTY** because `App.tsx` is touched by BOTH slice 1 and the nav flyout I

into it. Worth owning: I should have compared against the MOVED develop before pushing.

The flyout PR had restructured `App.tsx` into a declarative `appRoutes` table and already listed the checkout
routes - but as `role: 'return'`, and its render logic was:
```
const authRoutes    = appRoutes.filter((r) => r.role === 'auth');
const guardedRoutes = appRoutes.filter((r) => r.role !== 'auth');
```
so `return` routes rendered **inside** the AuthGuard - which is precisely the bug slice 1 exists to fix. A textual
merge could not express that; the fix had to be re-stated in develop's new idiom:
```
const publicRoutes  = appRoutes.filter((r) => r.role === 'auth' || r.role === 'return');
const guardedRoutes = appRoutes.filter((r) => r.role !== 'auth' && r.role !== 'return');
```
plus the map switched to `publicRoutes`, and a comment saying WHY (a buyer returning from Stripe has no account
yet; guarding that route bounces them to a login page for an account that does not exist).

now **never** triggers an abort, only a report.

budget** ends it, and the **launch probe** already refuses to start a run on a dead span. Costing one episode

## Tick 04:03 - a real launcher bug found behind a false alarm I correctly discarded
Counting bindings per model showed `nemotron-3-super` and `syn:large:vision` at **6 each against Synthetic's
ceiling of 5**. My first read was "over the ceiling". **That read was wrong, and I checked before acting on it.**
A BINDING is not a concurrent request: each run has exactly ONE active role at a time, so a model bound in six
runs is only in flight where it is the *currently active* role. Measured actual in-flight:
`syn:large:vision` **3**, `nemotron-3-super` **2**, `kimi-k3` **1** - all comfortably under 5. **Nothing is
breached.** That is the fourth false alarm tonight from the same family (truncated field, crashed grep, diff
direction, and now a proxy metric read as the real one), and the fourth caught by measuring rather than reacting.
**But the concentration underneath it was real, and it had a cause worth fixing.** Three of four launches this
session went to **trio 5**, which is how three concurrent executors ended up on one model. The reason is a genuine
bug in my launcher:
```
n,k,qw,ws = active()      # k = COUNT OF LIVE KIMI RUNS
...
roles = _trio(k)          # ...used as the ROTATION INDEX
```
`k` is a population count, not a counter. It is incremented per launch *within* a cycle, but re-read from
`active()` at the top of every cycle - so near CAP it barely moves, the index sticks, and consecutive launches all
land on the same trio. The table's concurrency spread was computed assuming trios get used evenly; this quietly
broke that assumption.
**Fixed:** added `_SEQ`, a monotonic launch counter, advanced **only on an actual launch** so a held task does not
skip trios, and used for both the initial pick and the probe-failure rotation. Launcher restarted, all six trios
passed the backend check, single instance confirmed.
**Worth stating plainly:** the alarm was false and the bug was real, and they were not the same thing. Had I acted
on the alarm I would have rebuilt the trio table again - the fourth rebuild tonight - and left the actual defect in
place, where it would have kept concentrating load until it did breach the ceiling.

**AND IT EXPOSED THAT MY 03:22 FIX WAS TOO BROAD.** I had just made the watchdog skip aborting any run whose
binding had "ever worked", because a probe queues behind a busy executor. **That reasoning holds only for a
SINGLE-SLOT backend.** The local span is single-slot, so the probe genuinely competes with the executor. Synthetic
is multi-slot: the probe runs on its own slot and IS diagnostic there. As written, my rule would have shielded
exactly this run - top priority, genuinely degrading model, seven completed rounds - from the abort it needed.
Narrowed: the exemption now applies **only** to single-slot local backends (`qwen3*` / non-`:synthetic`). On a
multi-slot cloud backend a failed probe still counts. Watchdog restarted, single instance, reading a live executor
at 1.3s and taking no action.
Two fixes to the same file in thirteen minutes, in opposite directions - the first was right about the local span
and wrong to generalise from it. **The physics of the backend, not the shape of the symptom, decides which rule
applies.**

because it is missing, but because production minification renames identifiers. **String constants survive

symbol name. Getting that backwards would have produced the same false negative by a different route.

## Tick 03:22 - MY WATCHDOG KILLED A HEALTHY RUN. Found it, proved it, fixed it.
The watchdog fired a second time and aborted `9bb3c3da` (task 40). I checked it the same way as the first, and
this time **the abort was WRONG**.
| run | completed executor rounds before abort | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `ba2ca222` | **none** (0 of 2 rounds) | genuinely stuck - abort was correct |
| `9bb3c3da` | **three - 190s, 584s, 430s** | demonstrably working - **abort was a false positive** |
**WHY THE PROBE LIED.** The local span is a **single-slot** backend: one `qwen3.8:27b` at 65536 ctx across both
3090s, single-stream. While its executor is mid-generation, a probe **queues behind the very executor it is
probing** and times out at 12s. So the reading says "the span is busy" - which is precisely what a *working*
executor looks like. Measured minutes later with **zero runs bound to it: 1.36s, GPUs at 0%, load 0.73.** On a
multi-slot backend like Synthetic the probe is diagnostic; on a single-slot local one **it is a contention check
wearing a health check's clothes**, and I built the abort path without noticing the difference.
**THE FIX - the discriminator is PROGRESS, not latency.** A binding that has completed an executor round is
proven workable, so a later failed probe means contention. A binding that has never completed one has shown
nothing, and starvation is the likeliest reason. The watchdog now aborts **only** runs with zero completed
executor rounds; anything that has worked is reported, never killed. A run that worked and then genuinely dies is
left to its own round budget - **losing one round budget is far cheaper than killing work that is happening.**
Both original aborts remain correctly classified under the new rule: `ba2ca222` would still be aborted,
`9bb3c3da` would not. Watchdog restarted, single instance confirmed, immediately reading three live executors at
1.3s / 2.0s / 2.0s and taking no action.
**What this cost:** task 40 lost its round context and relaunched as `4a2dbd31`. Its branch and commits survived,
so no work was destroyed - but ~20 minutes of successful executor time was thrown away by my own tooling, and I
would not have caught it by watching the fleet look healthy.

**Also this tick: powerplatform #99 MERGED `94df0523`** - on FRESH evidence, not the stale tick. After the branch
update it rebuilt at **09:49:57Z** (develop's last move was 07:33:10Z), compare read **ahead 3, behind 0**, and I
re-confirmed develop had not moved again before merging. CI lane `34339668563` running on develop.
Fleet: 6 running, 13 queued, no run failed since 08:00Z.

## Tick 02:41 - THE WATCHDOG FIRED FOR THE FIRST TIME, it was right, and its number changed the table
Run `ba2ca222` (task 16a) was aborted and requeued automatically. I checked whether that was CORRECT rather than
treating an autonomous abort as self-justifying.
**The decision trail is the design working, not a hair trigger:**
```
02:34:51  cold probe failed, WARM RETRY also 12.0s -> FAIL    strike 1/2, no action taken
02:36:20  89 seconds later, probed again -> FAIL 12.0s        strike 2 -> ABORTED + REQUEUED
```
Four probe attempts across two rounds, 89s apart, every one at the ceiling.
**Then I verified the verdict independently:** a direct 300-token call to `qwen3.8-nothink` returned 200 in
**111.5 SECONDS**. The span was genuinely starved. The abort was right, and task 16a went back to its own queue
slot with nothing lost - which is exactly the outcome the abort-and-requeue design exists to produce.

**The number it produced changes the table: TWO harness executors on the span is already too many.**
The span is effectively a ONE-executor resource while it also serves the CI eval gate. The launch probe gates the
moment of launch but cannot stop a SECOND run landing on the span afterwards - which is precisely how this run
starved. **Local-executor trios cut from 4 to 2.** Fewer starvations to catch beats a watchdog catching more of
them. That is a reduction in ambition against a measured number, not a retreat from Paxton's "local qwen3.8 for
ALL executors": the span physically serves about one, and asking for four guaranteed the failure that then had to
be cleaned up.
**Constraints re-verified after the edit, not assumed:** 6 trios, every one 3-distinct; `glm-5.2` **never** an
executor (demoted 02:10 after an 1800s timeout); max Synthetic concurrency **4** against the ceiling of 5; and -
new - **all six trios are DISTINCT configurations**. The naive balanced table a solver produced had identical
pairs, where a probe failure rotating to "the next trio" would have retried the same three backends and learned
nothing. Launcher restarted, all six trios passed the backend check, single instance confirmed; task 16a
relaunched on trio 4 at 1.3-1.7s.

## Tick 01:52 - TWO Synthetic models have degraded, and the standing "cut the scope" rule was WRONG here
Run `82b6aa62` (task 53) hit the 3-consecutive-failed-rounds gate. The standing rule says a run that loops three

task to work around a slow model.** The tell was in the shape: a DIFFERENT role timed out each round -

roles; bound backends do. So I probed before cutting.

|---|---|---|
| `syn:large:text:synthetic-anthropic` | **69.4s** | degraded - removed |

Neither removed model is DEAD - both return correct 200s. They are removed for failing their **role's time
budget**, which is a sharper and more useful test than whether a model responds at all: a 69s auditor cannot
finish inside 900s of real audit work, and that is exactly the timeout that killed round 2.

sweep.

models measured then - `syn:large:text` itself read cold 12.47s / warm 1.97s at 00:05 and is now 69s. Both things

it too broadly.

### FINDING 2 - the key is VALID but ORG-SCOPED, and that is why it still fails

I did not stop at "secret present". Triggered a real review on mcp-tools #36 and read the job:

    ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: ***          <- resolving now; it was blank before
    "type":"result","subtype":"success","is_error":true
    "duration_ms":271, "num_turns":1, "total_cost_usd":0, "modelUsage":{}

Zero cost and empty modelUsage on turn 1 means the API rejected the call - nothing was ever billed.
Probed the key directly (1 max_token, no content):

    HTTP 400 invalid_request_error
    "This API key is not scoped to a workspace, so this request must include the
     anthropic-workspace-id header with the ID of the workspace to use."

**400, not 401. The key authenticates - it is an `sk-ant-api0...` key and it is good.** It is an
ORG-level key, and `claude-code-action` sends no workspace header, so every call dies on turn 1.

Two fixes, either one closes it:
  A. Create a WORKSPACE-SCOPED key in the Anthropic Console and overwrite the secret. No workflow
     change, fixes both repos at once. **Recommended.**
  B. Keep this key and add `anthropic_workspace_id: <id>` to `claude-code.yml`. The action does accept
     that input - it is in the valid-input list the run printed. Needs the workspace ID.

Both need Paxton: the ID and the Console are his. **This is no longer "create a secret" - it is one
Console action, and the diagnosis is exact.**

## TICK 20:00 PT 2026-09-09 - #132 MERGED. THE REVIEWER FIXED ITS OWN BLINDNESS.

### The review of #132 confirmed the diagnosis AND found what the fix was missing

Verdict: *"diagnosis is sound, the fix is the right one (not just a workaround)"*. It also answered
the `fetch-depth: 0` vs `git fetch origin main` question better than I had framed it: an explicit
fetch **only fixes comparisons against main** and would silently reintroduce the bug for a sibling
branch, a tag, or another PR. `0` is durable for a job whose entire purpose is judging arbitrary repo
state.

### Not a stall - but reading it properly exposed a real defect

The log's newest line said `20:06` while its mtime was 20:16. **That is not a frozen log**: `now` is
stamped ONCE per cycle at the loop top, so every line in a pass carries the pass's start time. The
20:06 cycle was still writing at 20:16.

Which is the finding. **That cycle took TEN MINUTES**, and this is why:

    20:06   emit-probe nebo-outbound-first-response [LOCAL-ONLY] qwen3.8=12.0s qwen3.8-nothink=12.0s
              || BLOCKED: manager 12.0s read timed out; executor 12.0s; auditor 12.0s
    20:06   HOLD nebo-outbound-first-response - no trio had all three backends emit within 3s
    ... and the same three-model 12s timeout for EVERY remaining queued task, one after another.

**~20 queued tasks x 3 models x 12s = about 10 minutes of a single cycle spent hammering a backend
that was already saturated** - and every one of those probes was known-doomed the moment the first
one failed, because the span cannot change state mid-pass.

**Worse than waste: the launcher was competing with itself.** The span runs
`OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=2` - one slot held by the run it had just launched (task 88), the other
consumed by this probe storm. Task 88 has sat at r1 with **exec_len=0 for 11 minutes**. I cannot
prove the probes are the whole cause, but the launcher generating 60 timing-out requests against the
same two-slot backend its own executor is waiting on is not a theory - that is what the log shows.

### The fix: a per-cycle circuit breaker

    _LOCAL_SPAN_BUSY=[False]        # reset once per cycle
    if _LOCAL_SPAN_BUSY[0]:
        print("  SKIP (local span already failed a probe this cycle)"); continue
    roles=QWEN; rdy,rep=roles_ready(roles)
    if not rdy: _LOCAL_SPAN_BUSY[0]=True

One failed local probe now short-circuits the rest of the pass. Cycles return to seconds, and the
span stops being flooded by work that was never going to launch.

**`ast.parse` caught my first attempt before it was written** - I had inserted the reset between a
one-line `try:` and its `except`, which would have crashed the launcher on start. The file was never
modified; the parse check runs before the write, deliberately. Re-placed after the `active=` print,
outside the try. Backup `launch_queue.py.bak-202127`.

### THE FINDING: "never two runs on one working tree" is ADVISORY, not enforced

LongHorizon-Harness **#7** carries THREE P1s from `chatgpt-codex-connector`, all about workspace
reservation. Rather than just reading them, I checked what `main` does today:

    grep main/service.py for: same workspace | workspace_busy | already running.*workspace
                            | workspace.*conflict | active_workspaces
    -> NOTHING. Zero matches.

**`main` has NO workspace-level mutual exclusion at all.** It has reservation logic for `run_id`
idempotency - 38 references - but nothing stopping two runs entering the same checkout.

**The only thing enforcing that rule today is a client-side check in MY launcher script:**

    if os.path.basename(j["workspace"]) in {os.path.basename(w) for w in ws}: continue

So the invariant this whole operation is run by - the one I check every tick and quote in every task
file - **is a convention held up by one line of Python on this workstation.** Anything that POSTs to
`/api/runs` directly bypasses it entirely. PR #7 is what would make the SERVER enforce it, via
`_workspace_reservation_path` and a 409.

### And that makes the review's first P1 far more serious, not less

  *"Treating a reservation owned by `self_pid` as stale defeats mutual exclusion for the normal
  deployment, where concurrent HTTP handlers and the queue launcher run as threads in the same
  server process."*

**A same-PID marker is the NORMAL case in this deployment, not the stale case.** So #7 as written
would ship enforcement that is defeated in exactly the topology we run - and that is *worse than no
enforcement*, because the fleet would then trust it. Needs a unique holder token or an in-process
lock.

Second P1 compounds it: the resume path closes the reservation context before `_launch_worker()`,
leaving a window for another supervisor to take the same workspace. The create path already does it
correctly, so it is a consistency fix.

Third is independent and worth keeping: continuation proceeds from a torn state when round N is in
`rounds.jsonl` but its checkpoint never landed - precisely what the guard exists to reject, and the
release checklist says it must 409.

Posted all of it on #7 with the operator context, because a reviewer reading only the diff cannot know
that `main` has no enforcement and therefore cannot know what is at stake in getting this right.

This repo's lane **restarts CT110 and kills every in-flight run**, so it merges in a chosen window.
Merging mutual-exclusion enforcement that has a known hole in its mutual exclusion, during a window
that costs the fleet, would be the wrong use of that window.

### The DNS/certificate item is STILL REAL - and my recorded version of it was incomplete

Probed **from the CT210 runner** - the host that actually fails - rather than from here:

    pihole.lan          A     192.168.21.3
    pihole.lan          AAAA  fda9:27ff:f875:4d64:be24:11ff:fe2c:af61
    getent hosts pihole.lan -> the AAAA (IPv6 wins)

    resolver on CT210: nameserver 192.168.21.3  (the Pi-hole is also the DNS server)
    pihole.lan is NOT in /etc/hosts - it is a DNS answer

So the item stands: that name answers with a self-signed `CN=pi.hole` where every other internal name
gets a real Let's Encrypt cert, and a check expecting the latter can never pass for it.

**But my stored version said "192.168.21.3 self-signed CN=pi.hole" - only the A record.** There are
TWO records, and **the client prefers the IPv6 one.** So the obvious remedy - delete the A record -
would leave the AAAA answering, the check would keep failing, and it would look like the fix did not
work. That is the same shape as the database-clear ask I withdrew an hour ago: **an instruction that
is wrong in a way that only shows up after someone acts on it.**

### hydra #5 - a revoked device token comes BACK TO LIFE on the next deploy

**Two reviewers found this independently**, from different angles - `chatgpt-codex-connector` at
`auth.js:67` and Copilot at `auth.js:29`:

    loadTokenFile() only OVERLAYS onto the env-seeded DEVICE_TOKENS map, so a deleted id is re-added
    by the seed at boot and the file never removes it. The revoked credential is valid again.

**The worst shape a revocation bug can take**: it appears to work, the operator moves on, and the
credential quietly returns. And this repo's deploy recreates the orchestrator as a matter of course -
I read that job earlier tonight - so "any routine container recreate" is the NORMAL deploy here, not
an edge case.

Copilot's third point sharpens it: compose seeds `fake-*` DEVICE_TOKENS by default, so **the first add
or rotate writes those placeholders into durable storage**, where they survive the env var being
cleaned up. A placeholder becoming a permanent credential by accident.

**Scope stated explicitly on the PR**: this is a correctness defect in UNMERGED code, not a
credential-rotation discussion. That topic is closed by Paxton's decision and I am not reopening it -
but a revocation path that does not revoke is ordinary engineering and belongs in review.

## TICK 21:10 PT 2026-09-09 - FOUND WHY THE FLEET WALLBOARD HAS BEEN EMPTY FOR A DAY

### The deploy paid for itself within twelve minutes

PR #11 existed to make fleet registration diagnosable in one command. It was deployed at 20:58. By
21:10 it had produced a complete root cause for a fault that had been invisible for over a day.

    /api/meta          fleet_last_error = HTTP 413
    journalctl         "fleet reporter rejected /harness/heartbeat: HTTP 413"  x3, every ~5 min

### THE CAUSE - `server.py:659-682`

    def _heartbeat() -> tuple[list[dict], int, int, int]:
        runs = []
        for item in registry.run_items():        # <-- EVERY RUN EVER. No filter, no limit, no window.
            runs.append(build_run_summary(item, state=state))

`reporter.py:392` then gzips that and POSTs it **every 30 seconds.** Measured on the live registry:

    total runs      265      (cancelled 170 · failed 92 · completed 1 · incomplete 2)
    raw JSON     2,552,100 bytes   (2.55 MB)
    gzipped        763,205 bytes   (763 KB)
    per run           ~9,630 bytes

**Only 0-6 runs are ever active. The other 259 are finished work being re-transmitted every thirty
seconds, forever.** The payload grows monotonically with history and never shrinks. At some point it
crossed the receiver's body limit, the wallboard went dark, and **nothing anywhere said so** - the
header pill kept reading "connected".

That is the exact failure PR #11 was written against, and it is a good illustration of why: the
defect was never that it broke. The defect was that breaking was invisible.

### Queued as task 114, with the fix direction stated and one thing explicitly forbidden

`queue/747-114-fleet-heartbeat-413.json` -> 5,842-byte task, appended at the END of the 7xx band.
Duplicate-checked first: nothing in the queue covers it.

**"FIX THE SENDER. DO NOT RAISE THE RECEIVER'S LIMIT."** Raising the limit buys weeks and then fails
larger and harder to diagnose. A wallboard needs current state, not an archive. Also forbidden:
pruning run history to shrink the payload - **the registry is the record, the heartbeat is a view of
it; fix the view.**

Two further asks written in, both of which matter more than the immediate fix:
  - **make the payload size observable** - `_send()` already computes `original_size`; surfacing it
    means the next growth is visible BEFORE it 413s
  - `_send()` treats any 4xx as fatal, which is right for auth and **wrong for "too big"** - a 413
    should shrink and retry, not leave the node permanently unregistered. Told it to PROPOSE this
    rather than necessarily build it.

And it must verify against **both** `/api/meta` and `fleet.easybutt0n.ai/api/fleet/nodes` - because
`/api/meta` alone is the harness's own opinion of itself.

### Task 77b UNBLOCKED - its gate is met, and it inherits the finding

77b was blocked on exactly one condition: *"GET /api/meta must expose fleet_configured /
fleet_ever_succeeded / fleet_last_ok / fleet_last_error."* **All four are live.** Moved back into the
active queue with the 413 carried forward, and one instruction added: the fleet registers zero nodes
today for a now-known reason, so **an e2e test of it SHOULD FAIL, and must be written to fail honestly
on an empty list rather than softened to pass.**

### hydra #24 carries SIX P1s, and this page WRITES CREDENTIALS TO PRODUCTION HOSTS

`feat(fleet): Env and keys page in the Hydra web UX`, +3388/-5 across 18 files. Four of the six fail
loudly. **Two fail silently and destructively**, and those are the ones that matter:

**1. `catalog.js:434` - production writes go to the WRONG MACHINE.** Selecting prod for powerplatform
executes against `pp-dev-uat`/CT163 and writes `/opt/powerplatform-prod/.env` THERE, **reporting
success.** The catalog note directly above that line already says production is on a separate host;
the code just does not use it.

**This estate has already been bitten by exactly this shape.** Powerplatform prod is served by the
corsairai300 HOST stack, and a stale decoy container set runs identical names with months-old data -
querying the decoy first is what once made a live production record appear not to exist. **This would
reproduce that confusion with a WRITE instead of a read.**

**2. `env-service.js:276` - key verification never tests the submitted key.** The pasted `value` is
not sent; it only checks the local Ollama can generate. **So an invalid key verifies successfully -
and the documented rotation flow REVOKES THE OLD KEY AFTER VERIFICATION.**

Paste a bad key -> reported verified -> the working key is revoked -> the service authenticates with
nothing. **We are currently running on 1 of 7 Ollama keys**, so losing a working one is not a
theoretical blast radius today.

The other four, all real: the orchestrator Dockerfile does not copy `packages/env-catalog`, so the
built container **exits with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND at startup** - the control plane does not boot, not
merely the feature; production wiring passes no `pct` so even `GET /fleet/env` 500s; GitHub paths omit

documented restore flow restores what you just replaced.

## TICK 2026-09-10 04:02 PT — "BLOCKED, no reviewer workflow" was wrong for pp. #106 is MERGED.

### The mislabel
I had #105 and #106 recorded as **BLOCKED - powerplatform has no `claude-code.yml`, so the
review rule cannot be satisfied by any action of mine**. That reasoning was wrong. The absence of
the `@claude` workflow means **the bot cannot review it**; it does not mean the PR cannot be
reviewed. **I can read a diff.** BLOCKED is for "cannot advance until something else lands", and
nothing had to land here - I simply had not done it.

### #106 (task 108) PR -> REVIEWED -> MERGED -> LANE
Reviewed by reading the diff, not the description. **The change is good and implements two standing
estate rules correctly**, which I recorded on the PR:
  - `probeLiteLLM` uses `/health/liveliness` **with** the Bearer key. The bare gateway `/health`
    fans a completion out to every configured model, paid and GPU. This PR gets it right AND leaves
    the reason in a comment so it is not "simplified" back.
  - `probeBillingAdapter` uses `/api/health`, not the unmapped bare `/health` that 404s and once
    showed a live adapter as `degraded`.
  - the tests assert the **red** path (`fetchStatus = 500` -> `unavailable`), not only the green one.

**FINDING POSTED** - `probeAuthService` accepts `status >= 200 && status < 500` as healthy, and that
band **includes 404**. Its two siblings use `canReachJson`, which is strict `res.ok`. So a renamed
route or a wrong `PUBLIC_APP_URL` yields *"Auth service reachable - healthy - HTTP 404 (probe token
rejected as expected)"* - false, and false in exactly the way this PR exists to eliminate. Narrowest
fix is `&& res.status !== 404` plus a 404 test beside the existing 500 one. **Judged NON-BLOCKING
and merged anyway**, deliberately and on the record: the probe it replaces was a hardcoded

Re-probed before acting. Three identical probes: **200 in 0.020s / 0.013s / 0.015s.** Thirteen
milliseconds is impossible for real inference, so I did not treat it as health - the router runs a
**response cache** and an identical prompt is served from it. Re-probed with a UNIQUE prompt each
time, which the cache cannot serve:
    glm-5.2:synthetic-anthropic       200 in **1.308s / 1.306s / 2.004s**
    nemotron-3-super (control)        200 in **0.884s / 1.127s**
**glm-5.2 is healthy and comparable to its siblings.** The 04:33 launcher timeouts (12.0/10.0/12.0s)
and my 04:36 40-second timeout were **transient**, and they line up with the router restart at
11:17:55Z - the same cause as the 04:14 hold. Three sources agreeing on a symptom is not the same as
three sources agreeing on a diagnosis: all three of mine were sampling the same restart window.
**Fourth time tonight that not acting was the correct action.** Had I edited the trio table I would
have demoted a working model and blamed it for our router's crash - and the change would have looked
justified afterwards, because the table would have "fixed" a problem that had already gone away.

### THE REAL FINDING: my probe was the defective instrument, not the model
An identical-prompt probe against this router is **not an independent sample**. This is RULE 1's
"verify the reader before trusting the reading" in a new place, and it cuts both ways - it can make
a slow backend look instant, and it can make a DEAD backend look alive by replaying an old success.
**The launcher already gets this right**, and its comment says so:
    # A unique prompt per probe guarantees the request actually reaches the backend.
    body=...{"max_tokens":32,"stream":True,"cache":{"no-cache":True},
             "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Say READY (%s)"%nonce}]}
So `emit_ok()` is sound - nonce AND `no-cache`. The fault was in my ad-hoc curl probes.

### FIXED: `served_model()` was cache-vulnerable, in the one function where it matters most
`launch_queue.py:286` sent a **fixed `"hi"`** with no nonce and no cache bypass. Its docstring:
*"Ask the router which model actually answers for this alias (message_start reports it)."* If the
response comes from cache, `message_start` reports the model that answered LAST time - so the
diagnostic built to catch **"an alias silently serves another model"** could confirm an alias as
correct using a stale reply. Patched to nonce + `no-cache`, matching `emit_ok()`.
    backup           `launch_queue.py.bak-0440-servedmodel`
    `ast.parse`      OK; `uuid` already imported (line 5)
    line endings     bare-LF count **49 before and 49 after** - introduced none into a CRLF file
    diff             **only** the intended hunk (286-287 -> 286-296)
    launcher         pid **28464 unchanged, matched=1** - NOT restarted
**Deliberately not restarting the launcher**: three runs are live and the queue is draining, and my
own restart earlier tonight wiped `_PREV_SYN_DOWN` and defeated the recovery ramp. The edit applies
at the next natural restart; nothing depends on it sooner.

      * NO env-var support. **NO TESTS.**

      cli.py +27   types.py +20   **tests +140** (test_character_limits_config.py 89,

## TICK 2026-09-10 05:16 PT — started the caps port, STOPPED on a trap. Recording it, not guessing.

I set out to build the reconciled branch this tick. I stopped before editing anything, because
reading the code turned up a correctness trap that the "obvious" port walks straight into.

### TRAP 1 - scope: `run_default` is not reachable where the config is built
    cli.py:398   `def run_default(name, fallback)`  - NESTED inside the parser builder
    cli.py:1639  `config = HarnessConfig(...)`      - inside `_run_command(args)`
Different scopes. So "port `run_default` into the constructor" - which is what I prescribed at 05:12
- **cannot be done as written.** `run_default` reads `run_defaults = load_run_defaults()`, the
`.lh-harness/config.toml` loader, and that dict does not exist in `_run_command`.

### TRAP 2 - the obvious workaround SILENTLY KILLS their env-var feature
The tempting fix is to give the three flags a real argparse default:
    default=run_default(dest, <HarnessConfig default>)
That is how every other option in this CLI works, so it looks right. **It is not.** Theirs then does
    if args.auditor_output_chars is not None: config.auditor_output_chars = args....
With a non-None default that condition is **ALWAYS true**, so the CLI value is assigned every time -
overwriting whatever `__post_init__` had just read from `LH_HARNESS_*`. **Env-var support would
still be present in the code, fully tested, and completely dead at runtime.** That is precisely the
failure shape I have been chasing all night: a feature that looks wired and silently does nothing.

### The real design question, which is a decision not a detail
Correct precedence is **CLI > env > config.toml > default**. Getting it needs the code to
distinguish "operator typed the flag" from "argparse filled the default" - so `default=None` has to
stay, and config.toml must enter as a THIRD source applied only when neither CLI nor env supplied a
value. `__post_init__` cannot do it (it knows nothing about config.toml), and `_run_command` cannot
call `run_default` (trap 1). Options are: call `load_run_defaults()` a second time inside
`_run_command` (needs its own `ProjectConfigError` handling), or thread the resolved dict through
`args`. **Either is a real change to how this CLI resolves configuration, not a two-line port.**

### Decision: NOT hand-rolling this in a five-minute tick
The harness is the thing that runs everything else, two runs are live, and the naive version breaks
a feature while leaving its tests green. **Nothing was edited** - I created a scratch branch, read,
then deleted it; `git status` shows only the untracked guest-e2e doc. This is the fifth time tonight
that stopping was the right answer, and the first four were all cases where acting would have looked
justified afterwards.
**What changed this tick is the spec, not the code**: the 05:12 prescription "port `run_default()`"
is now known to be under-specified, and the trap that makes it dangerous is written down so whoever
implements it does not rediscover it by shipping a dead feature.

**Destination FOUND, not guessed:** the USB drive is `sdc` (TRAN=usb, 9.1 TB); its data partition

**The safety design is the ORDER and the task says so in capitals**: explicit cutoff -> EXPORT ->
TRANSFER -> **VERIFY ON THE DESTINATION** (checksum AND row count, re-read on terranas01, because an
scp exit code is not proof the bytes are readable at the far end) -> **only then DELETE**, bounded by
the SAME predicate rather than a fresh `now()` or it deletes rows written between the two steps that
were never exported. Plus: `DELETE` does not return space to the filesystem, and `VACUUM FULL` takes
an **exclusive lock on a table the live gateway writes to on every request** - so never unattended
on a 12-hour timer.

The consolidation's premise was "ornith good, qwen3.8/span bad". The earlier evidence was real -
`6eac2df7` showed qwen3.8 timing out twice as auditor at 1800s and once as manager at 1200s while
ornith completed both executor episodes. **But that was load-dependent, not capability-dependent.**

bottleneck; the span is comparatively idle.

whole fleet slower, not faster.** The ordering in the approved plan is therefore wrong: Phase 3 (the
second GPU instance) must come BEFORE the qwen3.8 cutover, not after it.
And that is blocked on RAM, which is blocked on freeing the span, which is blocked on the cutover.
**The cycle is real and it is a hardware constraint, not a config one.**

### THE FINDING THAT SETTLED THE WHOLE "MORE SLOTS" QUESTION
Freeing the span gave GPU1 14.7 GB free - and ornith reloaded with **`n_slots = 1` anyway**. VRAM
was never the cap. Ollama's own scheduler says why:
    level=WARN source=sched.go:509
    msg="model architecture does not currently support parallel requests" architecture=qwen35
    llama_context: n_seq_max = 1   |   llama_memory_recurrent: ... 1 seqs
**ornith is a hybrid SSM and CANNOT serve parallel requests at all.** `OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=8` is
set correctly and correctly IGNORED. So "4 slots" is impossible for this model, ever, at any
context size or VRAM - and **the only route to concurrency is more INSTANCES**. That makes the
second GPU not an optimisation but the sole mechanism, and it makes 256K free: each instance is
single-sequence regardless, so a bigger window costs no concurrency.

### The reviewer paid for itself on its first run, on the PR that argues for reviewers
It found a **real security defect in my own document**. The illustrative gate snippet read:

    ( author_association == 'OWNER' || 'MEMBER' || 'COLLABORATOR' )

In GitHub Actions expression syntax `||` **short-circuits on the first truthy operand, and a
non-empty string literal such as `'MEMBER'` is truthy** - so that condition is **ALWAYS TRUE**.
Anyone copying the snippet instead of the real file would have shipped a reviewer with **no
write-access gate at all**, invocable by any commenter - while the document's own verification
section claimed outside contributors were silently ignored. It reads correctly in English, which is
exactly what makes it dangerous. Replaced with the fully spelled comparison plus a boxed warning
that keeps the wrong form visible as a labelled counter-example.

The other three findings, all acted on: "four repos" -> three and the coverage table corrected;
`cognizioware-qa`'s default branch is **`master`** not `main` (targeting `main` opens a PR against a
branch nobody merges); and hydra re-framed from a coordination problem into a **quiet-window**
problem, naming the `deploy` job and the CT110 seeding wipe.

`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` is an **ORG** secret with **`visibility: all`**, set `2026-09-10T02:04Z`.

## Tick 11:45 PT 2026-09-10 - THE DUAL-GPU BENEFIT IS NOT REACHING THE FLEET, and I know exactly why

### Partial walk-back of my own claim
Task 123 is still VERIFIED as recorded: **`qwen3.8` and `qwen3.8-nothink` DO round-robin across both
