**But the harness does not run on those aliases.** Its degraded trio runs on **`ornith-1.5:pool`**,
and that alias is pinned to ONE card. Measured this tick, twice:

    live fleet traffic, last 6 min:   :11441 = 14 requests   |   :11438 = 0
    6 deliberate probes on the pool:  :11441 = 6             |   :11438 = 0
    nvidia-smi:  GPU1 94% util  |  GPU0 0% util, 22.9 GB resident and idle

So while I reported "the fleet now runs on both your GPUs", the truth is **the fleet runs on one GPU
and the second sits loaded but idle.** The capacity was delivered; the routing does not use it.

### Cause, isolated by controlled contrast rather than guessed
Three aliases, same two backends, one variable:

| alias | `:11441` | `:11438` | measured |
|---|---|---|---|
| `qwen3.8` | rpm=None | rpm=None | **4 / 4 even** |
| `qwen3.8-nothink` | rpm=None | rpm=None | both served |
| `ornith-1.5:pool` | **rpm=20** | **rpm=None** | **20+ / 0** |

`simple-shuffle` (the strategy actually in force - the DB row wins, file says least-busy) does
**weighted** selection over `rpm`. A deployment with no `rpm` carries no weight beside one that has
it, so `:11438` is never chosen. Every other field on the two pool deployments is identical - a
field-by-field diff showed only 5 differences: `api_base`, `mi_id`, `rpm`, and cost `0.0` vs `0`
(the same number).

### The fix - one call, no recreate, and it is BLOCKED pending Paxton's go
Both pool deployments are **DB-sourced (UUID ids)**, so this is editable live with no router
restart - exactly the property task 124 is migrating everything toward:

    POST /model/update
      {"model_id":"2ebf3ae9-850c-4289-a372-41074a2c0f4d","litellm_params":{"rpm":20}}

Setting `rpm=20` on `:11438` makes the weights equal. **Prefer this over deleting rpm from
`:11441`**: the cap was a deliberate choice ("rpm 20, not 40, because this is a shared daemon on a
shared card"), and `:11438` also serves the cloud relay and three embedding models, so a cap there
is if anything more appropriate. Current load is ~5 rpm, so a 20 rpm cap is not close to binding.

**I did not run it.** The auto-mode classifier blocked the write, and prod-box mutations need an
explicit go under the standing rules. Not worked around. **This is the single highest-value
outstanding action: it doubles fleet throughput at a moment when the local pool is the ONLY
capacity, and it is one reversible call.**

## Tick 11:51 PT 2026-09-10 - the rpm diagnosis confirmed from LiteLLM's own source, not inferred

Read `litellm/router_strategy/simple_shuffle.py` inside the running prod container:

    line 44:  weight = healthy_deployments[0].get("litellm_params").get(weight_by, None)
    line 46:  weights = [m["litellm_params"].get(weight_by, 0) for m in healthy_deployments]
    line 59:  selected_index = random.choices(range(len(weights)), weights=weights)[0]
    line 71:  item = random.choice(healthy_deployments)      # only when no weight/rpm/tpm at all

Two things make this bite:
1. It decides WHETHER to weight by inspecting **only `healthy_deployments[0]`**.
2. Every other deployment missing that key defaults to **weight 0**, not to an average.

So for `ornith-1.5:pool` with `:11441` first at `rpm=20`: weights `[20, 0]` -> normalised
`[1.0, 0.0]` -> **`:11438` has probability ZERO**. Matches the measured 20/0 and 6/0 exactly.
For `qwen3.8`, both deployments have `rpm=None`, so it falls through rpm -> tpm -> the uniform
`random.choice` at line 71 -> the even **4/4** measured at 17:52. **Two aliases, two code paths,
both predicted correctly** - this is no longer a hypothesis.

**It is also order-dependent**, which is why it was not obvious: had `:11438` been first in the
list, `weight` would read None and the whole weighted branch would be skipped, giving a fair split.
Fixing it by setting `rpm=20` on `:11438` makes the weights `[20, 20]` regardless of order, which is
the durable fix; removing rpm from `:11441` would work today and silently regress if ordering or
another rpm ever changed.

**STILL BLOCKED, unchanged:** `POST /model/update {"model_id":"2ebf3ae9-...","litellm_params":
{"rpm":20}}`. The auto-mode classifier refuses the write and prod mutations need Paxton's go.

### Considered and rejected: routing the degraded trio through `qwen3.8` instead
`qwen3.8` demonstrably round-robins, so pointing `DEGRADED_TRIOS` at it would get both GPUs without
touching prod. **Not doing it.** `active()` classifies any run whose blob contains `qwen3.8` into the
separate `qw` counter, which feeds a `LOCAL_CAP` branch (line 585) and the `trio="qwen"` path that
allows only ONE concurrent local run. That risks *halving* throughput rather than doubling it, and
it means re-verifying several interacting counters inside a file with documented patching hazards
while two runs are live. The launcher is currently stable and productive. The one-line prod fix is
correct, reversible and pending; interim churn is not worth the risk.

### 6. Three tooling bugs of MINE, all caught before they produced a false claim

 - **`scp -p 9222` silently used port 22.** In scp the port flag is `-P`; `-p` means "preserve timestamps".

 - **An inner `ssh` was consuming the OUTER ssh session's stdin**, killing the script before its VERDICT
   line. That is why two verify passes went silent at exactly the same point. Fix is `ssh -n`; I moved the
   verify to the MCP instead, which cannot hit the bug at all.

   SFTP. Transferred by streaming over `ssh` instead; the checksums prove the bytes arrived intact.

## Tick 17:32 PT 2026-09-10 - PR #140 REVIEWED. Real defect found. NOT merging.

### The review rule paid for itself today

`claude[bot]` finished in 4m 5s and worked all six requested items. This is the first substantive
automated review the pipeline has had, and it found something the overseer could not have.

### VERDICT: DO NOT MERGE. read-back-...fallbacks.py is BROKEN.

The script whose entire purpose is "a 200 is not proof, re-read the row and diff it" **cannot return
exit 0 against a real router_settings row**. Four compounding defects:

 1. SHAPE MISMATCH - `fetch_row()` returns the UNWRAPPED router_settings content (proven by
    prepare.py itself using `row["fallbacks"]` directly), but the expected body from
    `prepare --apply` is WRAPPED `{"router_settings": {...}}`. `flatten()` therefore produces key
    sets that NEVER intersect, so missing_keys/extra_keys fire unconditionally.
 2. The duplicate guard inherits it - `live.get("router_settings", {})` is always `{}`, so `dup_ok`
    is ALWAYS False regardless of the real DB state.
 3. Even fixed, the diff is UNSCOPED: the intended body holds only `fallbacks`, so every other live
    key (routing_strategy, num_retries, timeout, retry_after, allowed_fails, cooldown_time,
    allowed_fails_policy.*, context_window_fallbacks) reports as `extra_keys`. The docstring claims
    it verifies "no other key changed" but there is NO baseline to diff them against.
 4. The DOCUMENTED usage does not run - `prepare --apply` prints prose plus TWO json blocks into
    read-back's UNGUARDED `json.loads(raw)`, raising JSONDecodeError before the diff executes.

**Worse than missing a bad write: a genuinely SUCCESSFUL write also reports FAIL**, which could push
an overseer into an unnecessary retry or rollback of a good change.

### MY OWN VERIFICATION WAS INSUFFICIENT, AND I MUST CORRECT THE RECORD

At 17:29 I recorded the pre-merge build check as "COMPLETE and clean". It was clean - and it was
also incapable of finding this. It verified SYNTAX AND SAFETY, not CORRECTNESS:

    YAML parses          OK   - says nothing about logic
    guard exits, 0 tracebacks - AND THIS ACTIVELY MASKED THE BUG

Every script exits 1 on its `DATABASE_URL` guard BEFORE the diff path is reached. So the very result
I reported as reassuring - "refuses cleanly without credentials" - is the reason I never exercised
the broken code. **"It compiles and refuses safely" is not evidence the logic works.** That lesson is
written into task 142 so the next person does not repeat it.

### CONFIRMED CORRECT by the reviewer - recorded so nobody "fixes" them

 * prepare.py IDEMPOTENCE is correct - re-fetches the live row, appends only groups whose `source`

## Tick 17:55 PT 2026-09-10 - TRACK C durability landed; task 111 clears a full round

### The weekly trim is installed, and the naming was the part that could have failed silently

`/etc/cron.weekly/pve-ct-fstrim` on ptait07, 755, `sh -n` clean.

**It is named WITHOUT an extension on purpose.** `run-parts` silently SKIPS any filename containing
a dot, so `pve-ct-fstrim.sh` would have produced a cron job that looks perfectly installed and never
runs once - the exact silent-failure class this project keeps paying for. Verified with
`run-parts --test /etc/cron.weekly`, which lists the file, plus a dry check naming all five CTs it
would trim.

### WHY a cron and not `discard=on` - the evidence, not a preference

ptait07 ALREADY has `fstrim.timer` (last ran 2026-09-07, next 2026-09-14). It did not help:
`vm-100-disk-0` still read **99.87%** on 2026-09-10 while CT100 was ~23% used internally.

That is proof the host timer does NOT reach inside running containers - `fstrim -av` walks the
HOST's mounted filesystems; reclaiming an LXC's deleted blocks needs `pct fstrim`. Treating the
existing timer as sufficient would have left the problem exactly where it was.

The alternative, `discard=on` on each CT rootfs, was deliberately NOT chosen: none of the five disks
has it, and adding it requires restarting every container including the UAT router (CT204) and the
CI runners (CT210). That is downtime nobody approved, to achieve what a zero-downtime cron does.
Rollback is deleting one file.

### Paxton redirected me and he was right

For several ticks I reported "needs Paxton: the SMB password for the usbdrive share" as the one

That was correct and I should have seen it. The vzdump rescue EARLIER TONIGHT already ran over ssh
to terranas01 as prax211 on port 9222 with key auth. The credential already existed and was already
proven by work I had done myself. I went looking for a NEW credential for a NEW transport (a Proxmox
CIFS storage) when the working transport was in front of me.

A Proxmox *storage* was never the only way to stop dumps filling root.

### What was built instead: a vzdump hook

`/usr/local/bin/vzdump-ship-to-terranas.sh` on ptait07, 755, `sh -n` clean.

On `backup-end` it streams the archive to terranas01 over ssh, re-reads the SHA **and** the size AT
THE DESTINATION, and deletes the local copy ONLY if both match. Three safety properties, in order:

    1. NEVER delete an archive whose copy is unverified at the far end. A successful transfer exit
       code is not proof the bytes are readable there - that lesson is already paid for tonight.
    2. NEVER exit non-zero. A hook that fails can ABORT THE VERY BACKUP IT PROTECTS. Every failure
       path logs loudly to /var/log/vzdump-ship.log and leaves the local file alone.
    3. Only acts on backup-end; every other phase is a no-op.

### PROVEN TWO WAYS, because "I wrote the config" is not evidence

BEHAVIOUR, with a 12 MB synthetic archive:

    phase job-start    exit 0, file STILL PRESENT      <- correct no-op
    phase backup-end   exit 0, shipped + verified + local copy removed, in ~1 second
    log: "VERIFIED at destination (sha and size match) - local copy removed"

WIRING, by PVE's OWN PARSER rather than by re-reading my own file:

    perl -e 'use PVE::VZDump; ... read_vzdump_defaults()'
      ->  script => /usr/local/bin/vzdump-ship-to-terranas.sh

### A wrong path that failed SILENTLY, worth recording

My first attempt wrote to `/etc/vz/vzdump.conf`. **That directory does not exist on this host** - the
real file is `/etc/vzdump.conf`. The append failed, and had I not read the config back I would have
reported a hook that was installed, tested, and completely inert. The script was genuinely working;
the wiring was missing. **A passing behaviour test on an unwired hook proves nothing about
production.**

### Context that reframes the whole track

There is **NO scheduled backup job on ptait07** - no `/etc/pve/jobs.cfg`, and `vzdump.cron` holds
only a PATH line. The 18 GB that filled root were AD-HOC dumps (CT201 from June, CT204 from this
morning) that nobody moved. So this was never about taming a schedule; it is about catching manual
dumps, which is precisely the case that went unnoticed. A `script:` hook fires on ANY vzdump however
it is invoked, so it covers exactly that.

### ROOT CAUSE, read from the source

`check_synthetic_quota()` in ops-control-center/doctor/ops_doctor.py ~L1123 **DOES NOT ASK SYNTHETIC
ANYTHING.** Its own comments admit it: the API path is skipped ("we verified it doesn't work"), and
it falls back to a `psql` query against OUR OWN database -

    SELECT COALESCE(SUM(total_tokens),0) FROM "LiteLLM_SpendLogs"
    WHERE model ILIKE '%synthetic%' AND created_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL '7 days'

...compared against a HARDCODED `WEEKLY_QUOTA_TOKENS = 625_900_000`. That is a locally-summed token
estimate measured against an assumed ceiling, presented as the provider's own figure. Synthetic does
not meter in tokens at all - it meters REQUESTS PER 5H and a WEEKLY DOLLAR CREDIT.

### MEASURED - we were never close to the real limit

    requests last 5h : 66   against a cap of 500     = 13%
    requests last 1h : 47
    tokens last 5h   : ~370K

Regeneration alone is +5% of 500 every 15 minutes = **+25 requests / 15 min = +100/hour**. We were
consuming roughly HALF of what regenerates, while the launcher sat at DEGRADED_CAP=2 with 23 tasks
queued for an entire evening. **The capacity was there the whole time.**

### PER-ROLE COST - this answers Paxton's "use Synthetic only for the lowest-request agent"

    role/model                                  reqs   tokens    tokens/req
    syn:large:vision:synthetic-anthropic (exec)   25   243,891      9,756
    kimi-k3:synthetic-anthropic          (aud)    12    94,803      7,900
    nemotron-3-super:synthetic-anthropic (mgr)    26    31,466      1,210
    glm-5.2:synthetic-anthropic          (mgr)     3        45         15

The EXECUTOR is the expensive role - MORE tokens on FEWER requests. The MANAGER makes the MOST
requests and costs 8x less per request. So Synthetic belongs on manager+auditor and the executor
belongs on local ornith - which is EXACTLY what trios 0 and 1 already do. Trios 2-5 put the executor
on Synthetic and are the expensive ones.

## 2026-09-11 00:40 PT - DRAIN CLEARED; TWO CONSTRAINTS ON HOW FAST THE QUEUE CAN ACTUALLY DRAIN

DRAIN was cleared at 00:35 after containment was proven, #142 deployed and verified live, and the
launcher patched + restarted. Two structural limits were measured while waiting for the first tick,
and neither is a bug to fix tonight - they are the real throughput ceiling and should not be
rediscovered next tick.

### 1. THE CONCURRENCY CEILING IS **5**, NOT CAP=6

The one-run-per-workspace guard (line 611) compares **BASENAMES**, not full paths:

    os.path.basename(str(j["workspace"]).rstrip("/")) in {os.path.basename(...) for w in ws}

So `cognizioware-mcp-tools` and `/home/harness/work/cognizioware-mcp-tools` are treated as **ONE
tree**. Distinct full workspace strings = 6; distinct basenames = **5**. CAP=6 can therefore never
be reached from the current active band.

| tree (basename) | queued entries |
|---|---|
| **cognizioware-mcp-tools** | **19** |
| cognizioware-powerplatform-c | 3 |
| cognizioware-qa | 3 |
| LongHorizon-Harness | 2 |
| cognizioware-powerplatform | 1 |

**19 of 28 active entries funnel through a SINGLE slot.** That, not CAP and not backend capacity, is
what governs how fast the queue drains. **RESOLVED SAME TICK: the basename collision is CORRECT and must NOT be "fixed".** Verified on
CT110: `/home/harness/work/` contains exactly one `cognizioware-mcp-tools` directory, and queue
entries spell it BOTH ways (bare `cognizioware-mcp-tools` and the full
`/home/harness/work/cognizioware-mcp-tools`) while meaning the SAME checkout. Comparing full paths
instead of basenames would let two runs onto one working tree - the thing the guard exists to
prevent. All five trees the queue references exist on CT110, so no launch will die on a missing
workspace.

### 2. THE FIRST CYCLE AFTER A RESTART LAUNCHES **ONE** RUN, BY DESIGN

`_PREV_SYN_DOWN` is seeded **True** (line 190) specifically so that a restart forces the recovery
ramp. With Synthetic `ok`, the next cycle computes `_RAMP = True and not False = True`, prints
`RECOVERY RAMP`, and **breaks after a single launch** (line 766).

**This is deliberate and must not be defeated.** The code comment records exactly what happened when
a previous restart bypassed it: *"six runs launched into a brief recovery earlier tonight and five
died"*, including top-priority tasks 107 and 108.

**Consequence for Paxton's two-GPU ask:** `_SEQ=[0]` resets on restart, and trios **0 and 1 are the
only LOCAL-executor trios**. So launch #1 draws trio 0 (local, GPU A) and launch #2 - on the FOLLOWING
cycle - draws trio 1 (local, GPU B). **Both cards are expected to be working one cycle after the

## 2026-09-11 00:38 PT - MEASURED: THE ORNITH INSTANCES EVICT THEIR MODELS WHEN IDLE

Caught while watching for the first launch. GPU 0's resident memory fell **12,264 MiB -> 275 MiB**
with no run in flight. This is not a fault - it is Ollama's idle eviction - but it is a PRECONDITION
for "both GPUs earning their keep" and was not accounted for:

    :11438  /api/ps -> 0 loaded
    :11441  /api/ps -> ornith-1.5:9b-256k  11.3 GB  expires_at 2026-09-11T07:38:09Z
    nvidia-smi -> GPU0 275 MiB (evicted) | GPU1 12,252 MiB (about to expire)

**No `keep_alive` is configured** - not in the ollama unit files, not in the environment. Both
instances run as plain `/bin/ollama serve` (PIDs 544177 and 546030, up 9h44m).

**WHY IT MATTERS:** the local lane's concurrency comes ONLY from having two instances -
`ornith-1.5:9b` is a hybrid SSM (`arch qwen35`) with `n_seq_max=1`, so one instance serves exactly
one request at a time. If an instance is cold when the second concurrent run arrives, that run pays a
model load (~11 GB) before its first token, and the spread across cards can fail to materialise at
all.

**ACTION TAKEN:** both instances warmed with an explicit `keep_alive` via a normal `/api/generate`
call - **an API request, not a host configuration change**, so it stays inside the standing rule that
host-level changes on ptait01 need Paxton's explicit go. If residency needs to be permanent, setting
`OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE` on the two services IS a host change and must be asked for.

**Identical mechanism:** the four new lead items were inserted by REPLACING the anchor
`<ul>

re-append the anchor text it consumed - leaving an orphaned sentence with no opening tag.

did not prevent the repeat. Recording WHY, because "be more careful" is not a mechanism:

**The 01:32 fix worked because its verification included a NEGATIVE probe** - it asserted the orphan
fragment `</li>
 and passed it` was ABSENT. The 09:05 edit verified six things, all POSITIVE
(new content present, old dates gone, no skeleton tags) - and **not one of them could have detected
an orphan**, because an orphan adds no text and removes none. The probe set was blind to the exact
failure it was meant to catch.

**THE RULE, stated so it is mechanical rather than aspirational: when an edit REPLACES an anchor
rather than inserting around it, the verification MUST assert that the anchor's own text still
exists.** A positive-only probe set cannot detect consumed text. This now applies to every
string-replacement edit in this session - task files, queue notes, LEDGER entries and artifacts
alike, all of which are edited the same way.

**Repaired on the freshly-read file with both positive and negative probes**, including

## 2026-09-11 10:12 PT - BOTH WRITES FAILED SILENTLY-ISH, AND THE READ-BACK IS THE ONLY REASON I KNOW.

Creating the azure bypass PR server-side, **step 1 succeeded and steps 2 and 3 both failed**:

    1. create branch fix/azure-mcp-transport-on-main from main 234c88d0   -> OK
    2. PUT litellm-config.yaml   -> /c/Program Files/GitHub CLI/gh: Argument list too long
    3. PUT docker-compose.yml    -> /c/Program Files/GitHub CLI/gh: Argument list too long

**Cause: I passed a 112 KB base64 blob as a COMMAND-LINE ARGUMENT** (`-f content=...`). That exceeds
the OS argument-length limit. The Python that prepared the patch worked perfectly - it fetched the
file, asserted `count == 1` on the exact old line, and reported `patched -> 112321 bytes (delta +4)`.
**So the console showed a successful-looking patch followed by a failure on the line that actually
writes it.**

*** THE DANGEROUS SHAPE HERE IS THAT THE BRANCH DID GET CREATED. ***
A check that asked "does the branch exist?" would have said yes. A check that asked "did the patch
compute?" would have said yes. **Only reading the FILE back from the branch shows the truth:**

    693:    url: "http://azure-mcp-auth-proxy:3000"        <- still no /mcp
    349:      npx supergateway ... --port 3001"            <- still no --outputTransport

**The branch is byte-identical to main.** Had I reported "azure bypass PR created" off the branch
creation plus the patch arithmetic, that would have been a false claim with two supporting green
signals behind it. **This is the same class as the empty `git push` that published nothing, and the
same remedy caught it: read the artefact back, compare the line, never the message.**

**FIX: send the request body as a JSON file via `gh api --input`** instead of inline arguments. The
blob then travels through a file, not the argv. Retrying now, with the same exact-occurrence
assertion before each write and the same line-level read-back after.

## 2026-09-11 10:57 PT - CONFIRMED LAUNCHER DEFECT: THE all-Synthetic FALLBACK IS SILENTLY OVERWRITTEN.

Paxton asked which trio is working. Measuring that turned up a defect in the launcher's fallback
logic. **Confirmed by reading the control flow contiguously, not by inferring across a gap.**

**THE FLOW:**

    if trio=="kimi":
        roles=_trio(_SEQ[0])
        if ok<2 and not _SYN_DOWN[0] and (qw>=LOCAL_CAP or not _local_exec(roles)):
            roles=_trio_syn(_SEQ[0])                         # all-Synthetic selected
            print("  KEYS SHORT ... -> all-Synthetic trio")
        elif qw>=LOCAL_CAP and _local_exec(roles) and not _SYN_DOWN[0]:
            roles=_trio_syn(_SEQ[0])                         # same, SPAN FULL path
            print("  SPAN FULL ... -> all-Synthetic trio")

    # ---- OUTSIDE that block, the probe dispatch ----
    if trio=="degraded":   ... roles=_degraded_trio(...)
    elif trio=="qwen":     ... roles=QWEN
    else:
        for attempt in range(len(EXEC_POOL)):
            roles=_trio(_SEQ[0]+attempt)      # <-- OVERWRITES the all-Synthetic selection

**`trio=="kimi"` is neither "degraded" nor "qwen", so it ALWAYS falls into that `else`, and
`_trio(...)` discards whatever `_trio_syn(...)` chose.** The KEYS SHORT / SPAN FULL decision is
computed, announced in the log, and thrown away.

**PROVEN ON THE LIVE LOG:**

    10:23   KEYS SHORT (0 ok, local 2/2) -> all-Synthetic trio 711-69b-hydra-repo-dir-fix
    10:23   emit-probe ... [trio 1] glm-5.2=2.7s ornith-1.5:pool=11.7s syn:large:vision=1.3s

`[trio 1]` is `(_SEQ[0]+attempt) % len(EXEC_POOL)` and `EXEC_POOL=_TRIOS`, so that is **_TRIOS row 1
= glm-5.2 / ornith-1.5:pool / syn:large:vision - a LOCAL executor.** `_trio_syn(1)` would have
returned row 3 (nemotron executor). SYN_ONLY parses correctly as [2,3,4,5]; the table is sound. **The
selection is right and the dispatch throws it away.**

*** AND THE CODE DOCUMENTS THIS EXACT BUG CLASS THREE LINES AWAY. *** The `elif trio=="qwen"` branch
carries this comment:
    "2026-09-10 05:37: the first version of this fallback selected QWEN and then the rotation loop
     overwrote `roles` with _trio(...) anyway, so it probed Synthetic, was blocked, and launched
     nothing. Fixed by not entering the rotation at all when the trio is local."
**They fixed it for the local path by adding a dedicated branch. The all-Synthetic fallback still
falls through to the rotation and is still overwritten.** One bug, fixed in one of its two sites.

**WHY IT MATTERS - it is not cosmetic.** With `keys_ok=0` the launcher believes it is steering off the
contended local lane; it actually launches onto it. That is the precise mechanism the code's own
comments blame for killing task 67 three times and task 83 ("same role, same backend, repeatedly - a
backend fault, not scope"). It also explains today's 11.7 s probe and the 72 s local timeouts.

**MEASURED COST, from the runs in flight right now:**
    local ornith executor   task 143 round 1: **3600 s = the ENTIRE cli_executor ceiling**
                            task 153 round 1: 1648 s, auditor 1800 s (full ceiling)
    Synthetic executor      task 134 round 2: **421 s**
**Roughly 4-8x, and the local rounds are hitting budget ceilings rather than finishing.**

**NOT HOT-PATCHING IT.** Five runs are live and healthy. A launcher edit is inert until restart, and
a restart mid-cycle while it is managing five runs is not a change to make casually for a defect that
has existed for days. **Staged, appended to task 146 (the launcher-defect task, already in the active
band - no new task created), and raised to Paxton with a recommendation and a default.**

The 10:53 tick shows the all-Synthetic fallback behaving **correctly**, and that nuance matters more
than the original finding - because it is exactly what would make someone declare the bug fixed when
it is not.

    10:53   KEYS SHORT (0 ok, local 3/2) -> all-Synthetic trio 756-135-seq-powerplatform-prod-logs
    10:53   emit-probe ... [trio 4] nemotron-3-super=1.2s kimi-k3=1.5s syn:large:vision=...

All three Synthetic. So this cycle announced all-Synthetic and probed all-Synthetic.

**THAT DOES NOT REFUTE THE DEFECT - IT EXPLAINS ITS SHAPE.** The `else:` rotation still runs
`roles=_trio(_SEQ[0]+attempt)` unconditionally, discarding `_trio_syn(...)`. Whether the result is
all-Synthetic is **pure luck of where `_SEQ` happens to point:**

    rows 2,3,4,5  all-Synthetic   -> the overwrite is HARMLESS (4 of 6)
    rows 0,1      ornith executor -> the overwrite is WRONG     (2 of 6)

    observed 10:53  _SEQ -> row 4  all-Synthetic             <- correct BY COINCIDENCE

**So it misfires roughly ONE CYCLE IN THREE.** That is worse than a deterministic bug in one specific
way: **a single correct-looking cycle reads as proof it works.** Anyone verifying this fix by
watching one launch has a 2-in-3 chance of seeing the right answer from broken code.

## TICK #232 — 2026-09-16 02:05–02:12 PT — SCHEDULED TICK — **THE LAUNCHER WAS DEAD; THE PREVIOUS TICK'S OWN LEDGER EDIT KILLED IT**

**Actor identity established by ancestry, not by feel.** My claude.exe is pid 92516, parent pid 12840 =
`pwsh -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File C:\tmp\overseer_tick.ps1`, parent 3048 = `svchost.exe`,
parent 1752 = `services.exe` (Task Scheduler). **I am the scheduled ACTING overseer.** The
`START pid=12840` at 02:05:50 with no `END` in `overseer_tick.log` is MY OWN line. Acted, wrote, fixed.

### THE HEADLINE — LAUNCHER CRASHED AT 02:07:13, DEAD ~65 s, FIXED AND VERIFIED

`launch_queue.py` pid 67868 **died mid-cycle** at 02:07:13 with an unhandled exception, taking the whole
launch loop with it. Nothing would have launched again, ever, without a restart — and **no operator surface
shows a dead launcher**; it was found only because STEP 5 reads the log tail rather than trusting that a
process listed once is a process still running.

```
File "C:\tmp\launch_queue.py", line 618, in <module>
  j=json.load(open(f))
UnicodeDecodeError: 'charmap' codec can't decode byte 0x90 in position 2541
```

**CAUSE — AND IT WAS SELF-INFLICTED BY THE OVERSEER, ONE TICK EARLIER.** Tick #231 requeued task 103 and
wrote the provider's verbatim failure text into the queue entry's `note`, including the raw CJK
`Provider 限流或过载` (UTF-8 `E9 99 90 …`) and an em dash. `launch_queue.py:618` opens every queue JSON with
**no `encoding=`**, so Python used the Windows default cp1252 and `0x90` — the third byte of 限 — is
undefined there. Position 2541 in the traceback matches the first non-ASCII byte at offset 2539 in
`744-103-hivemind-booking-branch-merge.json`, measured, not inferred.

The irony is exact and worth recording: **NEXT TICK item (l) already warned that any fresh API reader needs
`sys.stdout.reconfigure(encoding="utf-8")`, and #231 applied it to its own reader — which is how it could
read and quote the Chinese text at all. The same tick then pasted that text into a file read by a
long-running process that had no such guard.** The rule was written for the overseer's readers and never
extended to the launcher's.

**BLAST RADIUS: ~65 seconds of launch outage (02:07:13 → 02:08:18), zero runs lost.** The two live runs
(`…T070917Z_0945b502`, `…T065253Z_7784478f`) are children of the harness service on CT110, not of the
launcher, and both were unaffected — confirmed still `running` after the restart. Because the launcher was
in `synthetic=DOWN` degraded HOLD, **nothing was waiting to launch in that window**, so the practical cost
was nil. Had this landed during a recovery window it would have silently held the entire queue.

**FIX — BOTH HALVES, BECAUSE EITHER ALONE LEAVES THE TRAP ARMED.**
1. **Durable (the real fix):** patched three unguarded opens in `launch_queue.py` (`.bak-tick232-encoding`
   taken first) — line 618 `json.load(open(f,encoding="utf-8"))`, line 784 `json.dump(…,open(f,"w",
   encoding="utf-8"),…)` (the WRITE side, which would have thrown `UnicodeEncodeError` on the same note when
   the task completed), and line 470 `keys_status.txt` with `errors="replace"`. `py_compile` clean.
2. **Defuse the live landmine:** rewrote task 103's note to ASCII —
   `[CJK xian-liu-huo-guo-zai = rate-limited or overloaded]`, em dash → `--` (`.bak-tick232` first). The
   meaning and the evidence survive; the byte that kills a cp1252 reader does not. Then **scanned all 55
   active + blocked queue JSONs**: 0 non-ASCII bytes, 0 parse failures. No second landmine.
3. **DEPLOYED, because a file edit is not a deploy.** Restarted through the `cmd /c … >> launch_queue.log
   2>&1` wrapper so the redirect is held (the 17 h frozen-log failure). **Exactly one launcher: pid 126116,
   parent cmd 129128, start 02:08:18.**

**VERIFIED BY READING BACK, NOT BY ASSUMING.** I did not call it fixed when the process appeared in the
list. At 02:09:33 the new process emitted a full status line and then **enumerated the entire queue,
including `hivemind-booking-branch-merge` — the exact file that killed its predecessor** — and holds it
normally. CPU advanced 0.109 → 0.172 s across 20 s and RSS 27.2 → 30.1 MB, so it is working, not hung.

## TICK #237 — SCHEDULED TICK — 2026-09-16 02:45:50 → 02:55 PT — `[1e0c8c]` — **I OVERTURN #236's HEADLINE REASONING, AND I DID NOT MAKE THE LAUNCHER CHANGE I HAD TALKED MYSELF INTO**

**Identity by ancestry, before STEP 0.** My bash `140784` → `92012` → `10024` `claude.exe -p "Run one
overseer sweep tick now…"` → `16988` `pwsh -File C:\tmp\overseer_tick.ps1` → `3048` svchost (Task
Scheduler). **Scheduled acting overseer.** The `02:45:50 START pid=16988` line with no END is mine.
Acted and wrote.

### CORRECTION 1 — #236's "exactly 3600s" argument carries NO information

#236's headline finding read: *"Both runs burned their executor budget to the exact second (3600s) on
round 1, on two different workspaces and two unrelated tasks. Two independent tasks do not become
oversized identically at the same second. That is a backend signature."*

**That reasoning is void. 3600s IS THE BUDGET** — `round.executor.started` carries
`{'budget': {'max_duration_seconds': 3600}}`, so **every** executor timeout is "exactly 3600s" by
construction. Observing it tells you the episode timed out; it cannot distinguish a backend fault from
an oversized task, because both produce the identical number. The auditor timeout is the same story at
its own budget (1800s).

**Blast radius, stated:** it was the stated basis for the standing "do not cut scope" diagnosis in the
ledger and for next-tick item (a), from 02:42 until this row (~13 minutes, one tick). Nothing else was
built on it, and **no run was cut or spared on the strength of it** — because the conclusion is
independently correct, see below. The wrong *reason* was live; the resulting *action* was right.

### THE CONCLUSION SURVIVES, ON DOCTRINE RATHER THAN ON ARITHMETIC

`…7784478f`'s round-3 executor timed out at **02:43:01** (3600190 ms). That is its **SECOND EXECUTOR
timeout** — round 1 at 00:54:40, round 3 at 02:43:01, same role, same run. The three-strikes
discriminator is explicit: *an oversized task moves its failure BETWEEN roles; a failing backend fails
the SAME role repeatedly. Same role twice = backend fault, do not cut scope again.* **So: no scope cut,
no injection, no round grant** — the same action #236 took, now resting on the discriminator instead of
on a number that was never evidence.

Full timelines, both runs, read from `/api/runs/<id>/snapshot` (`payload.phase`):

| run | ws | round 1 | round 2 | round 3 | now |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `…0945b502` | mcp-tools | exec **TIMEOUT** 3600s | exec **completed** 1366s, auditor **TIMEOUT** 1800s | exec started 02:20:17 | → expires ~03:20 |
| `…7784478f` | pp-c | exec **TIMEOUT** 3600s | exec **completed** 1913s, auditor **completed** 735s | exec **TIMEOUT** 3600s | exec started 02:44:15 → ~03:44 |

### THE CHANGE I TALKED MYSELF INTO AND THEN DID NOT MAKE

I built a case for lowering `DEGRADED_CAP` 2 → 1 and restarting the launcher, on two supports. Both
failed inspection, and I am recording them because the edit was one command away.

**Support A — the launcher's own comment.** `launch_queue.py:288`: *"I removed the :11438 ornith
deployment from the router, so there is now ONE ornith slot; a cap of 3 against one slot recreates
exactly the single-slot contention."* Same argument at a cap of 2, if there is one slot.
**MEASURED INSTEAD OF ASSUMED** — `GET /api/ps` on ptait01, both ports:

- `:11441` → `ornith-1.5:9b-256k`, 11.3 GB **resident in VRAM**, 262144 ctx
- `:11438` → `ornith-1.5:9b-256k`, 11.3 GB **resident in VRAM**, 262144 ctx

**TWO ornith instances are live.** The comment is **STALE** (dated 2026-09-10 02:15) and my memory note
`ornith-local-lane-db-owned` agrees: both :11441 and :11438 are DB rows. Had I trusted the comment I
would have **halved degraded-mode throughput on a false premise**, and the restart would have made it

**Support B — an overlap correlation, which is confounded.** I found that all four timeouts happened
while the other run's agent phase overlapped heavily, and both completions happened in the one window
where they barely overlapped (01:26–01:27). Tempting, and **wrong to publish as causal: longer episodes
overlap more BY CONSTRUCTION**, so "timed out" and "overlapped" are mechanically correlated whether or
not contention exists. Recorded as a **hypothesis**, not a finding.

**Net: no file edited, no launcher restarted, `DEGRADED_CAP` still 2.** An unverified premise is not a
licence to change a shared component at 3 a.m.

**The check that would settle it** (next tick, needs the LiteLLM master key): does the router's

### TICK #242 — SCHEDULED TICK — 2026-09-16 03:30→03:38 PT — pid 81312 / claude 105084

**Identity settled by ancestry before STEP 0, per doctrine.** Bash shell 134844 → `bash 83312` →
`claude.exe 105084` (`-p "Run one overseer sweep tick now…" --output-format text --dangerously-skip-permissions`)
→ `pwsh 81312` running `C:\tmp\overseer_tick.ps1` → `svchost 3048` (Task Scheduler) → `services.exe`.
**Scheduled acting overseer: act, write, resolve.** The `03:30:50 START pid=81312` line with no END in
`overseer_tick.log` is MINE, not a concurrent peer's — the failure mode that made four ticks stand down on
2026-09-15.

**Correction to #241's next-tick item (f), which told me to walk from the PowerShell tool's `$PID` because the
Bash route "returns GONE".** The Bash route is not broken — it is *transactional*. Each Bash tool call gets a
fresh `bash.exe` that exits when the call ends, so reading `/proc/$$/winpid` in call A and walking it in call B
always finds a dead pid. Read the winpid **and walk it in the same invocation** and it resolves the full chain
to `svchost` first time, which is what I did above. Both routes work; the rule is *one call, not two*. This
matters because #238 and #241 each lost part of a tick to a dead end that isn't one.

#### THE FINDING: `synthetic=DOWN` IS AN **OR** OF TWO CONDITIONS, AND EVERY TICK SINCE #236 HAS NAMED THE WRONG ONE

The launcher computes `_SYN_DOWN = synthetic_down() or synthetic_failing_real_work()` (`launch_queue.py:588`).
Those are completely different faults with completely different remedies — a provider 429, versus *two or more
`:synthetic` runs having failed in the last 1800 s* — and the status line collapses both to the single word
`DOWN`. Preceding ticks reported "Synthetic is down (~01:53)", dating it from **the last failed run**, which is
the `failing_real_work` branch.

**Measured, not assumed.** I evaluated `failing_real_work` myself against `/api/runs`: **0 hits in the window**;
the newest `:synthetic` failures are 01:39:04, 01:51:44 and **01:53:27**, all now more than two hours old and
long outside the 1800 s window. So that branch is **False** and has been since roughly **02:23**. The DOWN is
therefore coming from `synthetic_down()` — the real 429 probe — and has been for the last ~8 cycles.

**Both branches were true at the start and only one is true now.** The streak began at **01:36** (not 01:53),
when the three failures above put `failing_real_work` over its threshold of 2; that condition expired ~02:23 and
the 429 has carried the DOWN alone ever since. Twelve consecutive DOWN cycles (01:36, 01:51, 02:07, 02:09, 02:24,
02:39, 02:54, 03:10, 03:25, 03:40, 03:55, 04:10) = **2 h 34 m**, still below #249's ~18-cycle escalation

The same 429 body carries the router's **live fallback table**, and reading it unclipped corrected a fact this

the eleven pairs it could see. I captured the full 2,500-char body: the table is **22 pairs, not 11**.

  `qwen3.8--256k`, `qwen3.5:9b`, `qwen3.6`, `gpt-oss:20b`, `glm-ocr:latest` and `general-chat` are all keys
  without it. **Blast radius: in task 136's note from 02:24 to 04:17 PT (~2 h), never acted on, and it does not
  touch the acceptance test.**
- **SURVIVES, and is now read rather than inferred:** **zero `:synthetic-anthropic` keys in all 22 pairs.** That
  is the actual defect and the full table confirms it.

The PR sized the cap to azmcp's 15.7 GiB PEAK, but that peak IS the leak, so the cap preserves the incident rather than bounding it. Recommended 4g plus a 24 h working-set measurement, since azmcp's LEGITIMATE usage has never been measured; that is precisely why 122's remaining scope reads 'per-service sizing'. The memswap_limit lines are CORRECT and worth keeping: the browser services run mem_limit 2g against memswap 4g today, so their swap is unbounded at twice RSS.

- 2026-09-18 04:26 PT - INTERACTIVE [5321285c]: THE DEPLOY PATH IS BROKEN, AND THE BREAK WAS BEING LOGGED AS HEALTHY. Root cause, measured not guessed: optimistic_deploy_harness.py read the script with open(..., 'r') and passed it to subprocess.run(input=script, text=True). On Windows that stdin wrapper rewrites every line ending to os.linesep, so CT110's bash received carriage returns and died - 'syntax error near unexpected token' on the do of the for loop at line 27. The file on disk is CLEAN: verified 0 CRLF pairs and 74 line feeds. The corruption happened IN TRANSIT, inside that function. WORSE: the wrapper logged rc=2 as 'script aborted: a run started between our poll and its check. Correct behaviour - retrying later.' But rc=2 is OVERLOADED - the deploy script uses it for its own idle abort AND bash exits 2 on a syntax error - so a broken deploy read as a benign race, and would have read that way indefinitely.

Three changes: (1) the script is now sent as BYTES, so no newline translation can corrupt it in transit, with stdout/stderr decoded for the log; (2) the rc=2 log line now states that the code is overloaded and that the stderr must be read before calling it benign, citing this incident; (3) a new deploy_hold_reason() check refuses to start while C:/tmp/DEPLOY-HOLD-lh-harness.txt exists, printing the hold text into the log. (4) DIAGNOSABLE: the mode is carried into task 180's round-zero record, with the honest touch that it is OMITTED rather than guessed when the launch did not supply one.
